We convened the Security Council's first high-level debate on redressing historical injustice against Africa, placed conflict-related food insecurity at the center of its agenda, and with Guyana, co-drafted unanimously adopted resolution 2807 on youth, peace, and security. strengthening young people's role in conflict prevention and peace building. Mr. President, representation becomes meaningful when it changes decisions and improves lives. The imbalance within the Security Council is also present in international financial institutions. whose structures still bear the imprint of an earlier age. Developing countries need fairer voting power, stronger representation, and increased capital within these institutions, together with affordable finance, concessional resources, and fairer debt treatment. They must also participate equally in shaping the rules of international taxation. Sierra Leone, therefore, supports a UN framework convention on international tax cooperation. Through ECOWAS, Sierra Leone will champion a development system that responds more effectively to Africa's priorities. Mr. President, restoring trust and delivering for all must also embrace the unfinished cause of reparatory justice. In March, this Assembly adopted a resolution led by Ghana and supported by the African Union and Caribbean Community recognizing the trafficking and racialized chattel enslavement of Africans as the gravest crime against humanity. For Sierra Leone, this history is neither abstract nor distant. From Bonse Island in our own river estuary Thousands of Africans were forcibly transported across the Atlantic into enslavement. Freetown, our capital, would later become a home for formerly enslaved and liberated Africans. This history is woven into our national identity. However, The consequences did not end with abolition. Their legacy continues to be reflected in enduring disparities in wealth, power, and opportunity across our world. Reparatory justice is therefore not a plea for charity. It is a call for acknowledgement, former apology, the return of cultural heritage, fair redress, and guarantee of non-repetition. Sierra Leone stands with Africa, the Caribbean, and the wider African diaspora in advancing this cause, not to remain captive to the past, but to build a more just and equitable future. Mr. President, the same principle of fairness applies to Africa's critical minerals. Critical minerals are indispensable to the global energy transition. Yet too much value is still added elsewhere. Processing at source, fair value chains, technology transfer, and local industry would turn natural wealth into skilled work, stronger economies, and hope for our young people. The green transition must not reproduce the extractive time of the past. For the youth, this is immediate. A young person without work, opportunity, or a stake in the future becomes vulnerable to the recruiter, the smuggler, and the dangerous journey across the Mediterranean. Jobs, skills, and dignity are therefore part of any serious policy for peace and development. Mr. President, Sierra Leone does not ask the world what it does not demand of itself. We carry these same principles into our work at home. Through FID alone, we are increasing domestic food production and strengthening food security. Through free quality education, we are widening the path for the circumstances of a child's birth, from a child's birth to the future that awaits that child. In 2024, we enacted the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act and subsequently championed the proclamation of 27 November as the International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage. A girl in Sierra Leone is no more or less precious than a girl anywhere else in our beautiful world. Protecting her childhood education and freedom as part of what development is supposed to mean. A gas future, like the future of every young person, will be shaped by forces already remaking our world, climate change, artificial intelligence, and the energy transition. The meaning of for all becomes more urgent as we decide how these transformations will be governed. Artificial intelligence can improve, of course, education, health, agriculture, and public administration. It can also widen the inequality if infrastructure, knowledge, and rule-making remains concentrated in a few countries. Developing nations must help shape the standards that will govern technologies affecting their people. Climate change presents the same moral question in harsher form. Who benefits? Who decides? And who pays? In Shenge on Sierra Leone's southern coast, families watch the sea take their land, fishing grounds, and the graves of their ancestors. For them, climate change is the disappearance of home in the present. Those who contributed least to the climate crisis are bearing some of its gravest, greatest cost. Accessible and predictable climate finance, support for adaptation, and effective arrangement for loss and damage are obligations of justice. They are also investment in global stability Fairness in transformation depends on the institutions that govern it. Sierra Leone, therefore, supports the UNH initiative and wider reforms that make this organization more effective, accountable, and responsive. Efficiency matters, and reform must preserve the capacity to act. Mr. President, The choice of the next Secretary-General offers another test of institutional effectiveness and equality. In 80 years, every Secretary-General has been a man. The women put forward for this office have placed their competence beyond dispute. What remains is the will of the organization to live by the equality it asks of others and entrust a woman with its highest office. Mr. President, our insistence on a capable United Nations comes from experience. For Sierra Leone, this organization is part of our living history. It stood with us when our country was broken and helped us make peace durable. In this hall, a small state has the same vote as a great power. Imperfect as it is, that quality remains one of humanity's boldest promises. Sierra Leone will continue to contribute personally to United Nations peace operations, uphold international law, support mediation and peace building, defend the right of women and girls, and serve as a bridge wherever member states seek one. We will also continue to support the institutions of international justice. In this regard, Sierra Leone has nominated Professor Charles Cherno Jallow, a distinguished international jurist, to be endorsed by and has been endorsed by the African Union and ECOWAS for election as a judge of the International Court of Justice. We respectfully seek member states' support on the 3rd of November. Mr. President, the United Nations was created in a world of unequal power, yet it rests on a radical idea. Nations differ in size and strength, but their people do not differ in human worth. A United Nations that delivers for all makes that quality felt beyond this hall. Nearly 25 years ago, Sierra Leone placed their trust in peace because they believed tomorrow could be different. People around the world are asking something similar of us now. They need reason to believe that cooperation still works, that law still matters, and that promises made here will be honored in their lives. Let this session give them that reason. The world for all should not remain at the end of this year's theme. They must become the measure of our work.

I thank you all.

GAPGA

On behalf of the Assembly, I wish to thank the President of the Republic of Sierra Leone. The Assembly will hear an address by His Excellency Denis Bichir Owich, Chairman of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I request protocol to escort His Excellency and invite him to address the Assembly.

Bosnia and HerzegovinaChairman of the Presidency

Dear President of the United Nations General Assembly, respected Secretary-General of the United Nations, Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, It is an honor and a pleasure to address the 81st session of the UN General Assembly on behalf of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We are a symbol of a nation that has survived severe trials but has not lost its path towards a better future. In the period from 1992 to 1995, my country was subjected to aggression, joint criminal enterprises, genocide against Bosniaks, crimes against humanity, and other war crimes. Following the end of the aggression in 1995, destructive forces have sought through blockades, obstruction and other means to halt the progress of Bosnia and Herzegovina. They are slowing down our path towards a modern European state, but they cannot stop it. Today, Bosnia and Herzegovina stands at the doorstep of the European Union and the NATO. These are our strategic foreign policy objectives, unanimously defined by the state authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Unfortunately, there are still those seeking to realize greater state projects at the expense of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. During the aggression, they attacked our country by military means. Today, they do so by political, diplomatic and other means. It is very important that the UN courts have established the nature of the war waged against the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Final judgments, including those concerning joint criminal enterprises, have established that this was an international armed conflict. Judgments of the highest UN courts have established that genocide was committed against Bosniaks. They also stand as judgments on the greater state policies that, through a joint criminal enterprise, sought to divide and destroy Bosnia and Herzegovina as an independent, sovereign, indivisible and internationally recognized state. Ladies and gentlemen, we live in a world of injustice, insecurity and intolerance. The strengthening of authoritarian populism, the aggression against Ukraine, the suffering in Gaza, the war in the Gulf region, the catastrophic situation in Sudan and other flash points have brought humanity into a profound crisis marked by great uncertainty and fear. We must not remain silent in the face of injustice. The world did not respond adequately to the aggression against Ukraine and the genocide against Palestinians in Gaza, just as it did not during the aggression against Bosnia and Herzegovina. The aggression of the Russian Federation against Ukraine is a flagrant example of a violation of the UN Charter and international law, while Gaza is humanity's greatest defeat in the 21st century. The greatest global crises are directly interconnected and have the same root, the erosion of international law. Disrespect for international law cannot lead the world towards prosperity and a better future. Ladies and gentlemen, without identifying the causes of the crisis facing contemporary humanity, we cannot solve its problems. The politics of force cannot bring progress to humanity. Instead of force, we need respect and the strengthening of the existing international norms, rules and institutions that we have built over more than 80 years. The multilateral system today faces a serious challenge, a crisis of institutional trust. Trust is weakening because some actors in the international community undermine the values enshrined in the UN Charter. The future of humanity does not lie in policies of violence and human rights violations. Conflicts and wars are not the purpose of our civilization. Let us build a culture of dialogue, cooperation, and peace. In this context, I believe it is of utmost importance to reaffirm the importance of the UN Charter, revitalize the role of the UN as the global center for coordination and cooperation, support the reform process and strengthen the credibility of the United Nations, consistently implement the Sustainable Development Goals, build mutual trust, inclusiveness, and a democratic vision of leadership, and strengthen preventive diplomacy at a time of numerous tensions and conflicts. Let respect for international law, peace, solidarity, sustainable development, and justice be the path that we follow together. Ladies and gentlemen, We, in Bosnia and Herzegovina, call upon all UN Member States to focus on reaffirming relations between States on the basis of international law, ensuring respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms, promoting peace and social progress, combating hate speech and all forms of discrimination, strengthening policies for the prevention of genocide, crimes against humanity, and other war crimes; advancing the rights of women and children, and strengthening gender equality, better health care, and education. The world must return to the fundamental principles upon which the UN is founded: respect for human dignity, the sovereign equality of states, the peaceful settlement of disputes, respect for international law. These are not unrealistic propositions. They are the only possible foundations of a stable world. Bosnia and Herzegovina is a reliable and responsible member of the United Nations. Among other things, I would like to remind that Bosnia and Herzegovina is aware of climate change and committed to contributing to global efforts, committed to the transition towards renewable energy sources and the reduction of harmful gas emissions, and determined to combat all forms of terrorism. We in Bosnia and Herzegovina know that peace cannot be taken for granted. Peace must be safeguarded every day. It requires responsibility of political leaders, respect for the law, and readiness for dialogue. There must not be one standard for large states and another for small states. If we want to preserve trust in the international order, the rules we establish together must be applied equally. Ladies and gentlemen, Bosnia and Herzegovina is the only country in Europe where genocide was committed after the Second World War. In May 2024, the UN General Assembly adopted a resolution designating 11 July as the International Day of Reflection and Commemoration of the 1995 Genocide in Srebrenica. This resolution represents a profoundly moral and civilisational act by the UN General Assembly. The adopted resolution is equally important for the UN and for Bosnia and Herzegovina. It is particularly dangerous that the leadership of the Republic of Serbia glorifies the convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic. The monster Ratko Mladic is not a hero, but a convicted war criminal. The institutional glorification of this war criminal is an anti-civilisational and unacceptable act. It amounts to identifying Serbia's state leadership with one of the worst butchers in European history. It is an indication that Serbia has not abandoned the ideology and policies that lead to aggression and genocide. It is a direct assault on the values of the United Nations, whose court delivered a final judgment against this war criminal. Let me remind you that Serbia is the only state in the world that has been found by a UN court to have violated the UN Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide. I call on the United Nations and the European Union and other international actors to clearly condemn this conduct and take concrete measures against those who institutionally glorify convicted war criminals. Unfortunately, the ideology and policies that led to genocide against Bosniaks continue to threaten Bosnia and Herzegovina. From the podium of the UN General Assembly, I wish to publicly warn the international public that the current leadership of the Bosnian entity, Republika Srpska, continues to threaten the peace and security of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the region. We must stop this destructive policy together. The victims of the genocide and the employees of the Memorial Centre Srebrenica are facing unacceptable pressures from the police of the Republika Srpska. We must not allow that the police and other institutions of Republika Srpska, which committed the genocide against Bosniaks, today threaten the survivors and those that are preserving the memory on the victims of the genocide. Those seeking to destroy the Dayton peace agreement are attempting to create the conditions for the secession of the Bosnian entity Republika Srpska. In the period ahead, they will intensify their activities primarily with the aim of weakening and abolishing the mandate of the High Representative of the international community, which is also envisaged by the Dayton Peace Agreement, weakening the institution of the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and seizing the state property of Bosnia and Herzegovina, contrary to the national and international law. Ladies and gentlemen, Bosnia and Herzegovina is an unconquerable state. There is not a single map of Southeast Europe from the past 1,000 years on which Bosnia or Bosnia and Herzegovina does not appear. Bosnia and Herzegovina is home to people who love freedom more than their own lives. Finally, as the Chairman of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I wish to emphasize that I am proud of the brave people of Bosnia and Herzegovina. These are people who have suffered injustice, yet they continue to fight for justice. These are people who have been victims of lies, yet they continue to fight for the truth. These are people who support the struggle for justice, freedom, and human dignity throughout the world. These are the honourable and proud people of my homeland, Bosnia and Herzegovina. Thank you for your attention.

GAPGA

On behalf of the Assembly, I wish to thank the Chairman of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Assembly will hear an address by Her Excellency Sylvanie Burtone, President of the Commonwealth of Dominica. I request protocol to escort Her Excellency and invite her to address the Assembly.

DominicaPresident

Mr. President, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, my brother, good afternoon. I bring greetings to this Assembly from the people and government of the Commonwealth of Dominica. I congratulate you, Mr. President, on your election and on the theme chosen for this 81st session of the General Assembly: "Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations that Delivers for All". This theme speaks directly to the defining challenges of our time. We are living through an age of profound transformation. Technology is changing how we work, communicate, and understand the world. Climate change is reshaping economies, communities, and entire ecosystems. Conflicts are destroying lives and displacing families. Economic uncertainty is deepening inequality, while progress towards achieving the Sustainable Development Goals has stalled. These challenges are not unfolding in isolation. They are interconnected, global in scale, and beyond the capacity of any one nation to address alone. They demand stronger cooperation and renewed confidence in multilateralism. Yet, Excellencies, at the very moment when collective action is most urgently needed, this organization stands at a crossroads. The question before us, therefore, is whether we possess the courage, solidarity, and political will to shape that change and guide our world towards peace, justice, and shared prosperity. I strongly believe that most right-thinking individuals would agree that the UN system has substantially delivered for all countries over the several decades of its existence. For more than 80 years, This organization has embodied humanity's highest collective aspiration, that countries, large and small, rich and poor, can work together to prevent conflict, protect human dignity, and improve the lives of their people. The United Nations provides shelter and protection to people enduring conflict displacement, and natural disaster. It supports education, healthcare, peacekeeping, elections, and development in communities that might otherwise be forgotten. These achievements matter and must never be dismissed or diminished. What the United Nations does not currently do enough is deliver at the transformative level. Too often, humanity and the institutions we have created to serve us have had to concentrate on managing one crisis after another without giving enough attention to the conditions that allow them to persist. Excellencies, There is no question that managing crisis is necessary. It brings relief, restores hope, and saves lives. But we cannot stop there. Our responsibility must also be to address the root causes of these problems and build systems that are fairer, stronger, and better able to serve our people. The true test of this organization, therefore, is not only how well we respond after people have suffered. It is also whether we can work together to prevent that suffering in the first place. This is not to dismiss what has already been achieved. It is a call for us to build on that progress, strengthen our cooperation, and deliver the meaningful change that our people expect from us. A fundamental question that one must ask is, can the international system still deliver? For Dominica, this is not an abstract question. When a hurricane destroys our infrastructure, when international energy prices rise, when access to capital becomes more expensive, when global markets change, or when climate finance remains beyond our reach, the consequences are felt immediately in our homes, in our businesses, in our schools and hospitals, and in the very lives of our people. Yet, Mr. President, I do not come before this Assembly to speak only of vulnerability. I wish to speak of transformation and resilience. Dominica has made a choice. We have chosen not only to rebuild after disaster, but to build differently, build better, build stronger. We have chosen not only to adapt to climate change, but to demonstrate what a climate-resilient economy and country can look like. And we have chosen to move from dependence to greater resilience. Mr. President, in 2017, Category 5 Hurricane Maria demonstrated with devastating force the vulnerability of small island states like Dominica. The economic and human consequences were enormous. Hurricane Maria, however, also taught us an important lesson. Resilience should never begin after the disaster. Resilience must begin before disasters. The international community must therefore move from a model that primarily finances reconstruction after catastrophe to one that invests systematically in resilience before disaster strikes. For Dominica, this means resilient roads and bridges, resilient buildings, reliable communications, modern water systems, strengthened health infrastructure, and disaster-ready communities. But resilience is not only physical. A resilient country must have resilient institutions. It must have resilient public finances. It must have resilient energy systems, and it must have resilient food systems. Above all, A resilient nation must have people who possess the skills and confidence to withstand shocks and move forward. That is the Dominica that we are building. Excellencies, Dominica has begun the transition from imported fossil fuels to renewable energy. Our geothermal power plant is now in commercial operation and increasing the renewable share of our electricity generation to approximately 84%. We are well on our way to achieving 100% renewable energy by 2030. This is more than an energy project. It is economic transformation. It demonstrates that small states can lead in the transition to clean energy. Every barrel of oil that we no longer need to import strengthens our resilience to international price shocks. Every unit of clean electricity we produce strengthens our energy security. affordable, reliable, renewable energy can become a foundation for new industries, new investment, new employment, and greater competitiveness. The lesson is important beyond Dominica. We need international finance that recognizes the transformative nature of renewable energy investment in vulnerable countries. We need financing mechanisms that allow countries such as Dominica to move faster. And we need partnerships that allow the energy transition to become an engine of economic development and growth. Our ambition is not merely to generate clean electricity. Our ambition is to use clean energy to transform our economy. Mr. President, the international community has become very good at recognizing vulnerability. We have become less successful at financing the transformation that vulnerability requires. Too often, The cycle is predictable. A disaster occurs, infrastructure is destroyed, and economic activity collapses. We then mobilize resources to rebuild what was lost, often through borrowing that substantially increases debt to rebuild what we could have made more resilient from the outset. This is not an efficient financial model. The best time to build resilience is before disaster. The best time to finance transformation is before crisis. And the value of resilience should be measured not only by what we build, but by what we prevent from being destroyed. Mr. President, Dominica does not come to the United Nations asking to be treated as a victim of vulnerability. We come asking to be recognized as a partner in transformation. We must finance potential, not merely manage vulnerability. And this is not only about Dominica. It is about whether the global financial system is capable of recognizing a different development model. A model in which resilience is an investment, nature is an asset, connectivity is productive infrastructure, clean energy is economic opportunity, and prevention is financially smarter than reconstruction. That is the proposition we place before this Assembly. It is time that the international financial architecture evolves. Dominica joins its voice with those countries that continue to advocate for the use of multidimensional vulnerability as a practical and fair basis in determining access to development finance. We call for greater and easier access to concessional financing and grants for adaptation. We call for stronger disaster clauses in sovereign debt instruments. We call for financing mechanisms that can be activated rapidly when disasters strike. And we call for a fundamental shift in the way the international community views investment in resilience. Every dollar spent preventing the destruction of a road, a hospital, a school or a water system is an investment in future development. Dominica is prepared to serve as a demonstration country for this approach. We are prepared to work with international partners to show what happens when finance is designed around transformation rather than vulnerability. Mr. President, Dominica has long spoken of becoming the world's first climate resilient nation. Today, I wish to take that ambition further. We invite the international community to partner with us in making Dominica a living laboratory for climate resilience and sustainable development. Bring us the technology. Bring us the research. Bring us the investment. Bring us the innovation. And together, let us demonstrate what a resilient small island economy can look like. Resilient housing, smart and renewable energy systems, climate smart agriculture, modern water management, digital public services, resilient infrastructure, nature-based adaptation, and new industries powered by clean energy. This should not be a relationship based simply on donor and recipient. It should be a relationship based on partnership, innovation, and shared learning. Dominica has lessons to learn from the world, but we also have lessons to offer the world. Mr. President, transformation is ultimately about people. A resilient economy must create opportunity for young people. Young people want to inherit a country that is not merely protected from disasters, but one in which they can build businesses, work in new industries, participate in the global economy, and build meaningful lives at home. That is why our investment in energy, connectivity, digital transformation, tourism, agriculture, and resilience must ultimately converge around one objective, creating opportunity. Excellencies, The challenges before us extend beyond climate and finance. We meet at a time when war continues to devastate communities and ruin lives, when humanitarian crises are multiplying, when international law is under pressure, when trust between nations is strained. We cannot speak about development without speaking about peace. Without peace, development is tenuous. We believe in the principles of the United Nations Charter. We believe in respecting the sovereignty and territorial integrity of states. We believe in the peaceful settlement of international disputes. We believe in dialogue. And we believe that international law must apply equally to all nations and must be applied consistently. Small states must never become collateral damage in the competition among larger powers. The security of a small nation is no less important than the security of a large one. The credibility of multilateralism depends on fairness, but it also depends on delivery. The true test of multilateralism is not whether we can agree in this room. It is whether our agreements can transform lives outside of this room. That is why I welcome the central challenge of this 81st General Assembly, restoring trust. Excellencies, The world does not need another generation of promises that remain unfulfilled. It needs delivery. It needs institutions that respond faster. It needs financing that reaches vulnerable countries more efficiently. It needs partnerships that produce measurable results. and it needs a multilateral system that people can believe in again. For Dominica, restoring trust means closing the gap between international commitments and the lived experience of our people. It means ensuring that when the world says it supports climate resilience, resources actually reach the communities that need them. It means ensuring that when we call for sustainable development, financing mechanisms do not make sustainability harder to achieve. And it means recognizing that the challenges confronting small island states are not marginal issues. They are an early warning of the challenges that the wider world will increasingly face. The United Nations must remain a place where every country, large or small, can believe that its voice matters. But the United Nations must also remain a place where ambition can become action. Mr. President, we must also confront the serious challenges facing the Sustainable Development Goals. The SDGs represented a promise that by 2040, we would make meaningful progress in ending poverty and hunger, improving health and education, advancing equality, protecting our planet, and building more peaceful and inclusive societies. Today, that promise is at risk. Conflict, climate change, Debt distress, inflation, and persistent inequality have pushed the goals further out of reach for many developing countries. But this is not the time to abandon the 2030 agenda. It is the time to renew our commitment and concentrate on delivering results that people can see and feel in their daily lives. For Dominica, we have incorporated the SDGs as priorities in our National Resilience Development Strategy 2030, our Climate Resilience and Recovery Plan, and our wider development agenda. We see sustainability and sustainable development in the homes we have built for vulnerable families, in our investment in geothermal energy as cleaner, more affordable, and reliable energy. We see it in our efforts to strengthen education, expand technical and vocational training, and better prepare our young people for the world of work. We see it in our support for farmers, entrepreneurs, agri-processors, and tourism operators, who are creating jobs and building stronger local industries. We also see it in our work to protect our forest, marine resources, and natural environment. For Dominica, these resources are part of our identity but they are also essential to our food security, our tourism product, and the livelihoods of our people. Excellencies, The challenges before us cannot be overcome by any one country acting alone. They require a strong and effective United Nations, renewed international cooperation, and a firm commitment to multilateralism. We need a United Nations that does more than respond to crises after lives have been lost and communities destroyed. We need an organization that works with determination to prevent conflict, advance sustainable development, confront justice, and protect those who are most vulnerable. We need a system in which every country, regardless of its size, wealth, or influence, has a voice and a meaningful place at the table. We need multilateralism that is not selective, in its concern or even in its response, but fair, effective and responsive to the needs of all people. Our development must include young people, women and girls, indigenous peoples, persons with disabilities, the elderly and communities that have too often been left behind. If the United Nations is to deliver for all, it must first see, hear, and include all. Multilateralism is our best hope for addressing challenges that cross borders, threaten our shared future, and demand collective action. We therefore remain committed to peace, climate action, sustainable development, and the dignity of every human being. We remain ready to work with all nations in a spirit of mutual respect and shared responsibility to build a fairer, safer, and more resilient world. Mr. President, Let this 81st session be remembered as the moment when we collectively renewed our faith in cooperation and matched our words with action. Let this 81st session be remembered as the moment when vulnerability was met with solidarity, promises were honored, and trust was rebuilt through meaningful delivery. Above all, let this 81st session be remembered as the moment when this family of nations found the courage to act together and recommitted ourselves to ensuring that no country, no community, and no person was left behind. I thank you for the courtesy of your attention.

GAPGA

On behalf of the assembly, I wish to thank the president of the Commonwealth of Dominica. The assembly will now hear an address by his excellency, Guy Pamula, president of the Swiss Confederation. I request protocol to escort his excellency and invite him to address the assembly.

SwitzerlandPresident

President of the General Assembly, United Nations Secretary-General, Heads of State and Government, Your Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen, Switzerland is a country of mountains, valleys and different languages. Part of our history, therefore, meant learning to live with what divides us. We didn't make the mountains disappear. First, we learned to climb them, then to cross them. To do so, we built roads, bridges and tunnels. And we realized that a natural boundary is not necessarily a dividing line. It can also be a pathway that connects us. This very simple experience seems to me to have something to teach us about the world in which we live. because we are going through a time of upheaval. The international order established in the aftermath of the Second World War is under severe constraints. Conflicts are multiplying and becoming deadlocked. The most fundamental principles of the United Nations Charter, the prohibition of the use of force and respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity, are being openly violated. Added to this are transformations that are reshaping our societies. climate change and the increase in the number of disasters, humanitarian crises, inequalities, and also technological upheavals, notably artificial intelligence, which are often advancing faster than our collective ability to assess their implications. At the same time, multilateral institutions are having to respond to an increasing number of crises while facing pressure on resources and an erosion of trust. The theme of this 81st session of the General Assembly, Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation, a United Nations that Delivers for All, therefore aptly sums up the task before us. To restore trust, to support transformation, and to demonstrate through concrete results that cooperation remains possible. This erosion of trust extends far beyond the realms of peace and security. We're also seeing it in the global economy. Protectionism is on the rise. Supply chains built up over decades of interdependence are being reorganized or fragmented as a result of geopolitical tensions. The multilateral trading system has been weakened. and the WTO can no longer fully carry out some of its essential functions. Yet what is at stake here is not merely a technical issue of trade policy. The question is whether relations between states will continue to be governed by common rules, or if they will increasingly depend on the weight and power of each individual state. For Switzerland, This is a fundamental issue. That is because my country is an open economy with few natural resources. A large part of its prosperity therefore depends on trade, but also on the stability and predictability of the rules that make such trade possible. Economic resilience requires us to diversify relationships, forge new partnerships, and keep trade between different regions of the world as open as possible. This is particularly important for economies with fewer resources or limited market access. Access to markets, knowledge and technology can create opportunities that would not otherwise exist. These abstract concepts encompass quite concrete realities. A business that can take on an apprentice, a family that can secure a more stable income. A producer who can trade beyond their local market. Young people for whom the range of possibilities suddenly widens. That is also what we mean when we talk about a global economy. Trust is built when the rules offer everyone a genuine opportunity to participate. It is also built when states continue to engage in dialogue. Switzerland is neutral. This neutrality goes hand in hand with a steadfast commitment to the UN Charter, international law, and the UN's three pillars, peace and security, human rights, and sustainable development. Our experience has also taught us that dialogue is not a sign of weakness. Engaging in dialogue does not mean glossing over disagreements or abandoning one's principles. Engaging in dialogue means maintaining contact when positions begin to diverge. A bridge does not require the two banks of a river to become alike. It simply allows us to cross from one to the other. In times of tension, this possibility often becomes essential. Dialogue is a tool for de-escalation when crises erupt. Above all, it can serve as a means of prevention before crises arise. It is in this spirit that Switzerland will continue to offer its good offices and provide spaces where those who are no longer on speaking terms can, when circumstances permit, resume dialogue. Geneva is one such space. It is home to the UN, the WTO and numerous other international organizations, as well as scientific ones, humanitarian actors, representatives of civil society. and permanent missions of almost every country in the world. Every day, people from different backgrounds, representing interests that are sometimes at odds with one another, come together here. They do not need to agree in order to talk to one another. That is exactly what gives such a place its value. Switzerland will therefore continue as the host state to ensure that Geneva remains open, accessible and inclusive for large states and small, for the north and the south. But inclusion is not merely about having a seat at the table. It also means being able to make a real contribution to decisions that will affect one's own future. This is the case with international cooperation. Every society must be able to shape its future in accordance with its history, needs and priorities. Cooperation is not about imposing one's own values or a single model. It is valuable when it creates partnerships, facilitates the sharing of expertise and strengthens everyone's capacity to act independently. It is less about doing things for others than doing things with them. This principle takes on particular significance in the face of current technological revolutions. AI is the most obvious illustration of this. It offers considerable new possibilities in science, the economy, medicine, education, and the management of resources. But it also highlights the risk of a new divide between those who have the skills and infrastructure needed to participate in this transformation and those who are likely to feel only its effects. We must ensure that technological progress broadens opportunities without widening the gaps. This means that as many countries and societies as possible must be able to benefit from advances in AI, develop their skills and contribute to the debate on the rules that will govern its development and use. This is Exactly the aim of the Geneva AI Summit, which will take place on the 21st and 22nd of June 2027 under the motto, "Bridging Innovation and Trust." These two concepts must go hand in hand. Innovation in which societies no longer have confidence risks being rejected. Conversely, rules that would prevent all innovation would deprive us of enormous potential. Our responsibility, therefore, is to strike a balance to enable progress and promote its benefits while creating the conditions for the reliable and responsible development and use of these technologies. Artificial intelligence thus reminds us of a simple truth. Certain changes are so far reaching and so fast moving that no single state can manage all of their consequences by itself. We need institutions capable of dealing with issues that transcend national borders. We need multilateralism. But multilateralism will only retain its credibility if it is also able to evolve. Switzerland therefore supports efforts to reform the UN system as part of the UN80 initiative. This reform must make the UN more coherent, more effective and more results-oriented, while respecting the powers and responsibilities of Member States. The UN must focus its efforts where its action brings real added value, when problems transcend borders, when national or regional capacities are insufficient, or when a universal institution is needed to provide a common framework. The key question is therefore a simple one. How can we ensure that the resources, expertise, and energy invested in the multilateral system yield better results for those it is meant to serve. Because our institutions do not exist for their own sake, they exist for the people, for those who live in fear of conflict, for those who have lost their home following a disaster, for those seeking work or building a future for themselves, for the children whose lives depend on access to education and the new opportunities we are creating today. It is on this scale that the value of multilateralism is ultimately measured. Ladies and gentlemen, your excellencies, we cannot make the diverging interests of our countries disappear. We cannot erase disagreements, rivalries or borders, nor can we remove all of the mountains that stand between us. But we can determine how we wish to tackle them. We can preserve open dialogue rather than erect more barriers. We can keep the channels of communication open rather than resign ourselves to silence. We can ensure that technological progress creates more opportunities rather than new divisions. And we can reform our institutions rather than accept their gradual demise. Switzerland will continue to play its part using the means at its disposal, by upholding international law, promoting dialogue, providing its good offices, supporting effective multilateral institutions, and by remaining a country where the world can continue to come together and engage. We do not claim to have all the answers, but our experience in the Alps has taught us one simple thing. While a mountain might separate us, it can just as easily be crossed. Crossing it brings people together, coming together encourages dialogue, and dialogue fosters trust. Perhaps this is where our shared responsibility begins, to keep open the pathways that allow us, in spite of our differences, to continue moving forward hand in hand. Thank you very much for your attention.

GAPGA

On behalf of the assembly, I wish to thank the president of the Swiss Confederation. The assembly will now hear an address by his excellency Matthew Antonio Patrick Ormani, president of the Republic of Seychelles. I request protocol to his cause his excellency and invite him to address the assembly.

SeychellesPresident

Mr. President, Mr. Secretary-General, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, good evening. Mr. President, I warmly congratulate you on your election to lead the 81st session of this General Assembly. You assumed this high office at a defining moment for our Organization and for humanity. Seychelles assures you of its full support and wishes you every success in guiding our work. Mr. Secretary General, as this is the final General Assembly you will address in your current capacity, Seychelles extends its profound gratitude for your decade of dedicated stewardship. You have consistently championed a United Nations that is more effective, responsive, and grounded in the needs of the people we serve. Mr. President, the theme of this session strikes at the core of our contemporary global crisis. Trust has eroded, yet structural transformation is urgently upon us. In a world increasingly fractured by geopolitical rivalry, The answer cannot be a retreat into isolationism. It must be a revitalized commitment to multilateralism. The United Nations must prove that dialogue can bridge division, that international law must prevail over force, and that collective action achieves what unilateralism never can. Seychelles approaches the world guided by an enduring fundamental principle. We are a friend to all and an enemy to none. Our commitment to non-alignment is not a passive indifference. It is an active choice for peace. It is the conviction that principled democracy, diplomacy, mutual respect, and international law are the true foundations of global stability. Small states like ours do not seek strategic competition. We seek shared solutions. This requires a multilateral system that is principled yet practical, ambitious yet accountable, and representative yet effective. In short, a United Nations that delivers for all. If multilateralism is to deliver, it must first secure the peace upon which all human progress depends. Without peace, sustainable development is an illusion. Conflict destroys lives, uproots communities, and diverts vital resources away from healthcare, education, and climate resilience. We must reject the normalization of perpetual conflict and the selective application of international law. International law must apply equally to all, without exception, bias, or double standards. This

People is vital to maritime security. The oceans are the lifeblood of global trade. When maritime routes are threatened by piracy, geopolitical friction, or armed aggression, the shocks ripple far beyond regional waters, devastating vulnerable island economies. Freedom of navigation and maritime security must be preserved under international law. Small and vulnerable states like ours should never bear the collateral economic cost of conflicts in which you have no part. Furthermore, we firmly reject unilateral coercive measures that violate international law and inflict disproportionate hardship on innocent populations. Yet our global architecture is failing to reinforce these principles. because its key organs remain outdated. The Security Council's inability to act decisively in moments of global crisis undermines its very purpose. Its composition reflects a bygone era, not 21st century geopolitical realities. Reform is no longer a matter of political convenience. It is a matter of institutional survival and legitimacy. Seychelles, therefore, reaffirms Africa's unified position. Our continent must hold no fewer than two permanent seats on the Security Council, with full prerogatives, including the veto, for as long as it exists. Mr. President, this past June, Seychelles proudly celebrated 50 years of independence. Half a century of self-determination has taught us a fundamental lesson. Size does not define sovereignty and geography does not diminish dignity. We may be a small island developing state, but we sit as an equal participant in this hall. Every nation regardless of population or economic power, possesses an inherent right to sovereignty, territorial integrity, and national dignity. Today, however, sovereignty faces quiet, insidious threats. Transnational organized crime, drug trafficking, and illegal, underreported, and unregulated fishing threaten our security. wreck our marine ecosystems, and steal from our people. Because these threats are interconnected, our response must be equally integrated. Stronger international intelligence sharing, expanded maritime surveillance, and practical law enforcement support. It is unreasonable to expect nations safeguarding vast oceanic domains with modest budgets to meet standards set by heavily resourced states without providing them the tools to do so. Resilience without resources is not resilience. It is merely survival. The same logic applies directly to the climate crisis. For Seychelles, climate change is not a prospective debate. It is a daily reality that strikes at the very foundations of our society. Rising seas threaten our infrastructure, our coastal livelihoods, and our very territory. The science is undisputed. The targets are clear. What remains missing is political will and execution. Major emitters must display greater ambition, while all nations act according to their responsibilities and capabilities. Economic growth that bankrupts the planet for future generations is not progress. Seychelles, therefore, welcomes the advisory opinion of the International Court of Justice on climate change, reinforcing that climate action is rooted in international law, equity, and intergenerational crisis. Mitigation, adaptation, technology transfer, and loss and damage funding are not acts of charity. They are legal obligations. Our survival is inextricably linked to the health of the ocean. Protecting our marine environment is an economic necessity. As an early ratifying state of the BBNJ Agreement, Seychelles looks forward to its first Conference of the Parties and urges all member states to finalize their ratifications swiftly. Yet, our ambitions are hampered by structural economic barriers. Frameworks like the Antigua and Barbuda agenda for seeds and the servile commitment must be backed by real capital. For small island states, that sustainability is a matter of national survival. We require affordable, accessible, long-term financing, meaningful debt relief, and the full implementation of the multidimensional vulnerability index. Measuring a nation's development solely by GDP per capita ignores extreme exposure to climate shocks and geographic isolation. If international finance is to serve reality, it must first measure reality correctly. Looking ahead, we must also address the rapid rise of artificial intelligence and emerging technologies. Whilst these tools offer immense opportunities for development and ocean management, They also risk widening the global divide and enabling new forms of warfare and cybercrime. We must ensure technology serves human dignity. We call for global digital governance anchored in human rights, ethical standards, and international law, with the United Nations playing a central role in steering this transformation. Mr. President, excellencies, across every crisis we face, one fundamental truth endures. Our ultimate duty is to the people we represent, our families, our youth, our coastal communities, and future generations. Our nations represent a rich tapestry of cultures, languages, and political systems. But diversity need not breed division. Guided by our policy of friend to all and enemy to none, Seychelles believes that our differences can be the dynamic foundation for stronger global cooperation. Let us restore trust through deliberate action, by upholding the rule of international law unconditionally, by reforming our global governance institutions to reflect today's world, by delivering equitable climate and development finance, and by protecting our shared oceans and climate. Seychelles enters this General Assembly with deep humility, clear conviction, and an unshakable belief in the multilateral system. We may be a small nation, but our voice, our sovereignty, and our aspirations will never be measured by our size on a map. Let this 81st session be remembered not for the divisions we inherited, but for the courage, solidarity, and resolve with which we overcame them. Let us restore trust. Let us manage transformation. And together, let us build a United Nations that truly delivers for every nation and every human being. I thank you, ladies and gentlemen.

GAPGA

On behalf of the assembly, I wish to thank the president of the Republic of Seychelles. The assembly will now hear an address by his excellency David Ranibook Adeyong, president of and head of state of the Republic of Nairobi. I request protocol to escort his Excellency and invite him to address the assembly.

NauruPresident

Mr. President, Mr. Secretary General, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, I bring you warm greetings from my people and my country. We meet under the theme, restoring trust, managing transformation, a United Nations that delivers for all. For my country, that means ensuring no nation, regardless of size or distance, is left behind as the world changes around us. Mr. President, let me begin by congratulating you on your election to preside over this 81st session. My delegation assures you of our full support, and we thank your predecessor for the stewardship of the 80th session. We also pay tribute to Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, This is the last General Debate of his tenure, and my country records its gratitude for a decade in which the smaller states were heard more often than before. I have traveled far to speak on matters that may seem distinct, but are united by a single fundamental principle: the right of every people to be treated as an equal and to speak for itself. Mr. President, there are moments in the life of a nation when its people are called to remember who they have always been. This is such a moment for us. And so I begin with something deeply personal to my people and my country, and that is our name. For many years, the world has known our country as Nauru. Nauru is how our name sounded to those who found it hard to say, and the world kept it. but it is not the name our people used among themselves. I rise on my first point not to announce a change, but to affirm a truth. Long before our country took its place among the family of nations, long before our name appeared on international records, our people knew our homeland by one name, Nauru. That name carries the memory of our ancestors, our language and our identity. It has been there all along, never lost, never absent. Today we restore Nauru. We did not make this choice to erase our past. We make it because we honour it. We do so with respect for our history and with gratitude for the journey Nauru has carried us through to our independence and our place on the international stage. Mr. President, My government's priority is investing in our people and our future generations. Restoring our name gives back to them a piece of the inheritance because the identity handed down by our own ancestors has a place in the community of nations. Because their history and language matter. Because they too have the right to inherit a nation that knows itself, names itself, and speaks of itself. In light of this year's theme, let me say this: there can be no genuine trust and no true transformation without respect for the identity, history, language and rights of every people to be treated as an equal and to speak for itself. I take the opportunity now to convey my sincerest gratitude to the Secretariat and to this Assembly and the many institutions and partners who have taken steps to recognize our restored name. It may seem a small courtesy, but it means a great deal at home. And so, Mr. President, I say this with the greatest pride. Ngaa de Naro. That means I am from Naro, and so is every person I have the honor to speak for today. We take our seats under that name, proud of where we have come from, confident in who we are, and determined to carry our name into the future. What I ask of the world costs nothing, Join us in recognizing and respecting the identity that is already ours. Say our name, Nauru. Mr. President, Nauru is an ocean state. We are not merely guardians of the ocean, but rightful participants in its future. For Nauru, the ocean represents both opportunity and responsibility, never one without the other. Both are essential. or the United Nations Convention of the Law of the Sea is left hollow. Today, I focus on a part of it that belongs to no one, the deep seabed area beyond national jurisdiction. Mr. President, the convention established the International Seabed Authority and charged it with a clear legal obligation to put in place regulations and regulate activities in parallel with sponsoring states. Its role is not to determine whether deep sea bed mining is, as a matter of public policy, a correct course of action. Nauru joined, trusting in the commitments set out in the Convention and the 1994 Agreement. For 15 years, Nauru has invested critical resources in sponsoring the exploration of a portion of the deep sea bed. Our sponsored entity, Nauru Ocean Resources, has contributed about one petabyte of data, more than one third of all Clarion Clipperton Zone data held in the authority's deep data. We called on the authority to seek an advisory opinion on the responsibilities of sponsoring states, and we followed it. We established a national regulator with the powers and due diligence obligations that opinion requires. At every stage, our decisions have rested on the best available scientific evidence, on the convention and on that opinion. At every stage, we have called for the mining code to be finished. And when progress stalled, we looked to the 1994 agreement and invoked the two-year rule. We were told then that we were rushing. That was five years ago, and today the rules remain unwritten. We are participating in the first contentious proceedings before the Seabed Disputes Chamber because our obligations as a sponsoring state require legal clarity. For 15 years, we have done everything a member state can do, consistent with our obligations as a sponsoring state, and today we continue to wait. Mr. President, there is a general understanding within the Authorities Council that nothing is agreed until everything is agreed. and that the regulations will be adopted by consensus. Achieving that is a great challenge for an institution whose members remain deeply divided on whether deep seabed mining should proceed at all, a question the Convention never asked the Authority to decide. NARO welcomes every effort to ensure that seabed mineral development proceeds responsibly. And I ask this Assembly to reckon with this. A principle declared in 1970 and a bargain struck in 1994, both in this Hall, still wait for the rules that would give them effect. When a multilateral process cannot deliver, the world does not stand still. Those with the means to act will not wait. And every year of delay makes that more likely, not less. That is why the theme of this session matters. A multilateral system that cannot deliver for a state like mine does not deliver at all. That holds here in this assembly and in any institution we build. Nairo therefore calls upon the authority. Let the waiting end. Adopt the rules. Similarly, Mr. President, a multilateral agency with which we see of increasing irrelevance to the NATO, namely the International Criminal Court, is one which calls for NATO to end its participation and to revoke its membership. Before I depart New York, NATO will be depositing our instruments of withdrawal with the Rome Statute repository. Mr. President, My government's central purpose is to put Nauru on its own feet. That work is underway. Our trust fund, to which we contribute more than 10% of our revenue every single year, so that Nauru has something to stand on when and if these arrangements end. Our fisheries, the seabed, joining the Egmont Group, new revenue through our investment and residence programs, A virtual asset regulator built with full due diligence obligations before the industry it regulates. Our valuable partnerships. And behind all of it, investment in health, education and sport, so that our people are not only better off, but healthier and better prepared. We are building an economy that does not depend on any single arrangement, and by every measure of fiscal discipline, we have done what was asked of us. Yet the measure by which we are assessed sees none of it. It sees income and it sees nothing else. It does not capture the full story of my nation. The true cost of our geographic isolation, the fragility of our limited economic base, or the devastating impact a single disaster can have on our people and our progress. In January 2027, Nauru will be considered a high-income country in the OECD system. That does reflect real progress, but progress should not be punished. Because 58% of our revenue comes from bilateral arrangements that are not ours to renew. 87% of the food our people eat is purchased and imported. We have one runway, one port, one road that connects everywhere. None of that appears in how we are assessed. That is why we strongly support the Multidimensional Vulnerability Index, or MVI, and the United Nations' efforts to pilot the tool. Its full implementation is essential to ensuring that countries like ours are fairly assessed and adequately supported. It recognizes that vulnerability is complex, and it must be seen, measured, and acted upon. Mr. President, we acknowledge the significant progress made by some development partners and financial institutions. in adopting vulnerability assessments and reviewing the eligibility criteria. The Asian Development Bank, ADB, weighs vulnerability alongside income, and its own policy names my nation as the clearest example of why income alone conceals what small island states face. As a country that is ranked the fifth most vulnerable country in the world on the index, and the most vulnerable in the Pacific, we welcome these developments as positive steps. But a gap remains. Not all have taken the necessary steps to truly recognize our realities. I therefore urge all who have yet to do so, including the World Bank, to weigh vulnerability alongside income in decisions on eligibility, as the ADB already does. If the international community is truly serious about restoring trust and managing transformation, it must demonstrate that commitment where it matters most, with those who are most vulnerable. Mr. President, I turn to my final point. No country of our size stands alone. Nairobi is a friend to all and an enemy to none. Nairobi's partnerships are not all of one kind. Some are born of kinship, some of shared interests. Some have been built through decades of cooperation. And some are grounded in the conviction that when a wrong persists, it must be named and addressed. Each relationship matters. None is a substitute for another and none comes at the expense of another. Mr. President, small states are increasingly asked to choose between partners, between blocs, between competing visions of the world. Nairobi will not be made to choose. We will work with every partner who respects our sovereignty and our right to decide our own future. That is not neutrality. It is called independence. Partnership does not mean agreement on everything. It means standing together where interests align and standing on principle where they do not. A friend I speak for today has been waiting for justice. I am asking this assembly to honor its word. And I cannot then fall silent when that word is broken for someone else. For 33 consecutive years, This Assembly has called for an end to the embargo against Cuba. NATO retracts that call, and we encourage dialogue grounded in full respect for sovereignty, because sovereign equality must be more than a principle written in the Charter. Whatever this Assembly intends to deliver, it will be delivered through partnership and cooperation, or not at all. So I extend an invitation to the members of this Assembly. Invest in our people, invest in our economy that rests on more than a handful of arrangements. Invest in institutions that will outlast my government and the next. Invest in the infrastructure, connectivity and opportunities that distance has too often denied us. What NARO offers this Assembly is not dependence, but participation. Not expectation, but contribution. Not a beneficiary, but a partner. Invest with us, not simply in us. Mr. President, I've raised today concerns to this organization and what it has promised. So does this. The Security Council does not reflect the world as it is. It reflects the world as it was in 1945, when most of the countries in this hall did not yet exist as sovereign states. NARU, therefore, calls for reform that expands both the permanent and non-permanent categories. A body that speaks for all of us should look like all of us. Mr. President, as I draw my statement to a close, the matters I've raised may appear separate. They are not. Our name is about sovereignty. How we are measured is about justice. The deep seabed is about opportunity and responsibility. Our partnerships are about standing as equals. One principle binds them. the right of every people to be treated as an equal and to speak for itself. You have convened this assembly to restore trust, to manage transformation, and to deliver for all. Trust is restored when promises are kept. Transformation is managed when decisions lead to action. And we deliver for all only when you deliver for the small. Everything NADRA has asked for today was agreed in this hall long before I took this floor. I am not asking this assembly to be braver than it has ever been. I am challenging you to be as good as your word. Say our name. Let the waiting end. Let vulnerability be measured honestly and treat us as partners. May God bless the Republic of Nauru. May God bless the United Nations. I thank you.

GAPGA

On behalf of the assembly, I wish to thank the President and Head of State of the Republic of Nauru. The assembly will now hear an address by His Excellency, Thieu Lam, General Secretary of the Communist Party of Vietnam and President of the Socialist Republic of Vietnam. I request protocol to escort His Excellency and to invite him to address the Assembly.

Viet NamGeneral Secretary and President

Distinguished guests, ladies and gentlemen, the world is undergoing profound shift in the international order with many risks and uncertainties. The tendency towards the threat or use of force and the arms race, especially the modernization of nuclear weapons and the development of new technology weapons, are heightening the risk of confrontation, miscalculation, conflict, and even of large-scale wars. At the same time, the global economy is becoming increasingly fragmented amid mounting barriers to trade, investment, and technology. Supply chain disruptions and economic instability are narrowing development opportunities for many countries. Climate change, natural disasters, pandemics, and emerging technological risk continue to pose direct threats to the lives of the people and their livelihoods, and to the development and stability of many nations. The shift in the balance of power and development inequalities are placing growing strains on international relations. Instability is further exacerbated when competition goes unchecked, commitments are left unfulfilled, and international law is applied selectively. An erosion of trust is further impeding efforts at cooperation. What should concern us is not only how the international order is changing, but where that change will take the world. Change is inevitable, for it is of the objective course of history. However, conflict and confrontation are not inevitable. From our own history, Vietnam understands the cost of war, the value of independence, and the power of reconciliation and cooperation. It is therefore my belief that the theme of this session, restoring trust, managing transformation, a UN that delivers for all, aptly reflects the urgent demands of the time. Distinguished guests, From the losses of the Second World War, humanity created the UN with the aspiration to prevent wars, safeguard peace, promote cooperation and place relations among nations on the foundation of common principles. Over the past eight decades, despite its limitations, the UN has helped sustain dialogue, advance decolonization, uphold the right of peoples to self-determination and support development. This must be preserved and carried forward Our institutions must be reformed to keep pace with the times, while fundamental principles of the UN Charter must be respected and reinforced. What we seek is a more equitable, democratic and inclusive international order, where every country has a voice and every nation has the opportunity to develop. The mission of our generation is to help shape and manage change so that competition does not turn into confrontation, differences do not lead to conflict, and advances in science and technology do not create new divides. In this spirit, I wish to put forward four key priorities. First, we must restore trust among nations on the basis of respect for the UN Charter and international law. UN Charter and international law form the foundation for the international order. They must be respected fully, consistently, and without selectivity. All states must respect each other's independence, sovereignty, territorial integrity, and right to choose their own path of development, refrain from interference in internal affairs, and refrain from the threat or use of force inconsistent with the UN Charter. Restoring trust does not require countries to erase differences, but rather to manage such differences responsibly. Crises must be prevented, competition must be kept under control, and dialogue must be sustained. Major powers should lead by example in respecting international law, exercising restraint, and responsibly addressing common challenges, and the UN must remain at the heart of these efforts. In every conflict, civilians must be protected, international humanitarian law must be respected, and humanitarian access must be ensured. Vietnam supports the right of the Palestinian people to self-determination and a two-state solution with an independent state of Palestine living peacefully alongside the state of Israel in line with international law and relevant UN resolutions. In the Asia-Pacific, nearly six decades of the ASEAN's development have demonstrated that countries can transform suspicion into trust, confrontation into dialogue, division into cooperation, and individual strength into collective might. In that spirit, Vietnam remains steadfast in its commitment to resolving disputes, including those in the East Sea, by peaceful means in line with international law, particularly the 1982 UNCLOS. Vietnam is resolute in safeguarding its sovereignty, sovereign rights and jurisdiction. The seas and oceans must remain spaces of peace, cooperation, connectivity and sustainable development. In the same spirit of peace and respect for people's right to development, Vietnam has always stood in solidarity with the state and people of Cuba. We call upon the US to end the unilateral embargo and sanctions and the energy blockade against Cuba and remove Cuba from the list of state sponsors of terrorism. We also call upon the international community to support Cuba in overcoming the sanction-induced crisis. Second, we must advance development that is equitable. Humane and inclusive and sustainable international commitments must be translated into action and bring people lives of peace, security, dignity and happiness. It is for this reason that the Pact for the Future and the 2030 Agenda, our promises to present and future generations, must be implemented earnestly and in full. Commitments on financing for development, including the severe commitment. must be translated into concrete measures, expanding access to long-term financing at affordable cost, supporting countries burdened by debt, and amplifying the voice of developing countries in international financial and monetary institutions. The multilateral trading system must be strengthened in an open, equitable, and transparent manner, ensuring development opportunities for all countries. Climate action must be accorded its rightful place in development cooperation, particularly via adaptation finance, technology transfer and a just energy transition. Development must be people-centered and leave no one behind. Growth must go hand in hand with social progress and equity, environmental protection and the safeguarding of people's livelihoods, especially for vulnerable countries and communities. global progress, must uphold the spirit of humanity in relations among nations, safeguard their legitimate interests, and respect differences in history, culture, and development conditions. Third, we must proactively shape technology governance so that progress serves humanity in our common development. Science, technology, digital transformation, and artificial intelligence are opening up unprecedented opportunities. but they're also presenting new challenges. The future of technology does not automatically guarantee equitability, and technological progress must help narrow divides and expand development opportunities, rather than creating new forms of dependency or new sources of conflict. We need to develop inclusive, safe, transparent, and accountable principles and governance frameworks to ensure that technologies will be in service of the people, while respecting national sovereignty, digital sovereignty, and the right to development. Developing countries must be able to participate substantively in rule-making, receive support for infrastructure and digital capacity, and enjoy equitable access to the benefits of scientific and technological progress. Vietnam's hosting of the signing ceremony for the UN Convention against cyber crime in Hanoi last year reflects our desire to make substantive contributions to global digital cooperation. Vietnam stands ready to work with partners to strengthen cooperation and build capacity in preventing and combating cyber crime so that people may live safely and benefit from technological progress. We also stand ready to support international initiatives on green and digital transformation and the development of effective governance framework so that science and technology can truly become drivers of shared development. Fourth, we must strengthen multilateralism and the essential, indispensable role of the UN. The strength of the UN does not lie in its ability to replace the responsibilities of state, but in its legitimacy and capacity to build consensus, establish norms, develop rules, and mobilize global efforts to address common challenges. For the UN to adapt to the transformations of the time, Vietnam supports efforts to reform the organization, particularly the GA, the Security Council, and the Secretariat, with a view to enhancing effectiveness, prioritizing structural reform, and streamlining the apparatus, while fully harnessing the UN's advantage in advancing global agendas and safeguarding the interests of developing countries. These perspectives are drawn from the experience of Vietnam itself. Over the past half century, since its accession to the UN mirrors the transformation of our own country. From primarily a recipient of invaluable assistance during the years of Doi Moi, Vietnam today is making proactive contributions to our common endeavors while deepening and broadening our substantive relations with the UN. Vietnamese military personnel and police officers have served and will continue to serve in UN peacekeeping operations. carrying our nation's aspiration for peace to places where peace remains fragile. Our tradition of independence and self-reliance provides a foundation for Vietnam to strengthen its strategic autonomy and proactively pursue international integration, looking towards our goal of becoming a developing country with a modern industrial base and upper middle income by 2030 and developed high-income country by 2045. Vietnam is establishing a new development model based on productivity, quality and added value with science, technology, innovation and digital transformation as key drivers with economic growth closely linked to cultural development, social progress and equity and environmental protection. Autonomy also means proactively adapting and cooperating with the world on an equal footing. Vietnam therefore pursues a consistent foreign policy of independence, autonomy, self-reliance, peace, friendship, cooperation and development and of multilateralization and diversification of external relations. Vietnam will remain steadfast in upholding the UN Charter and international law, promoting dialogue on the peaceful settlement of disputes and deepening its participation in UN peacekeeping missions. Vietnam is working with fellow ASEAN member states to build a united, self-reliant and resilient ASEAN and actively preparing to host APEC in 2027. And as a member of the UN Human Rights Council, Vietnam champions dialogue and cooperation in promoting and protecting human rights and in ensuring that all can share the fruits of development. We stand ready to share our experience in poverty reduction, agricultural development, and climate change adaptation to work with partners to broaden cooperation for common interest. The world will continue to change. The direction for such change will depend on the choices we make and the responsibilities we shoulder today. Vietnam chooses peace, cooperation and development, we will work steadfastly with all countries to strengthen the UN, uphold international law and translate our shared commitments into tangible benefits for our people. We believe that with a strong UN, together we can build a more peaceful, equitable, inclusive and better world for all. And on this journey, Vietnam will remain an active member, reliable partner and a responsible nation, always standing ready to contribute to the common endeavors of the international community. Thank you very much.

GAPGA

On behalf of the Assembly, I wish to thank the General Secretary of the Communist Party of Vietnam and the President of the Socialist Republic of Vietnam. We shall now continue the general debate. The assembly will now hear an address by his excellency Dear Gratios and Njambi. Vice president of the United Republic of Tanzania. I request protocol to escort his excellency and invite him to address the assembly.

United Republic of TanzaniaVice President

Your Excellency, Dr. Halil Rahman, President of the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly, Your Excellency Antonio Guterres, Secretary-General of the United Nations, Excellencies, Heads of State and Government, distinguished delegates, good afternoon.
