It is indeed a great honor and privilege to address this Assembly on behalf of Her Excellency, Dr. Samia Suluhu Hassan, President of the United Republic of Tanzania. Her Excellency, the President, asked me to convey her fraternal greetings and best wishes for the success of this session. Mr. President, allow me to congratulate you on your election to preside over the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly. Your immense experience and diplomatic skills give us confidence in your ability to guide the proceedings of this session successfully. Your election is also a fitting tribute to the great country, Bangladesh, with which Tanzania enjoys excellent relations. Mr. President, about 80 years ago, The United Nations was founded in San Francisco on a simple but enduring principle: that nations can prevent war and advance peace through trust, collective action, and respect the UN Charter. Today, war and insecurity are not only existential threats to our survival, but a range of challenges, including climate change, pandemics, un-governed artificial intelligence, and energy insecurity, just to mention a few. These challenges should remind us of a need for a stronger and much more coordinated United Nations. Therefore, the theme of this session, that is, restoring trust, Managing transformation, a United Nation that delivers for all, is timely for it requires us to revert to the founding principles of maintaining peace and restoring trust. Managing transformation requires reforming the UN to meet the realities of our time. In that regard, I commend our illustrious Secretary-General, His Excellency Antonio Guterres for championing the UN80 initiative that aims to advance the transformation agenda. In our opinion, the UN80 initiative must go beyond administrative efficiency to include overall organizational effectiveness, accountability, and representativeness for the United Nations to be able to deliver for all. Further, The transformation must be undertaken with utmost caution to avoid going off track on the development pillar and incapacitating the United Nation country offices and programs. Mr. President, Excellencies, and distinguished delegates, while we are a few years away from year 2030, progress towards attainment of the SDGs is still unimpressive. Given this situation, we need to improve our execution and ensure that every cent invested delivers results. Tanzania remains committed and has made strides in implementing the 2030 Agenda. Tanzania's Development Vision 2050 aims to build an inclusive and competitive economy that ensures quality of life for all. We are investing in our people, productive infrastructure, technology and innovation, while creating greater opportunity for women and young people. Our ambition is to transform economic growth into lasting improvements for people's lives. These ambitions may not be realized if the international financial architecture is not made to work for development. Currently, when developing countries are accelerating progress, they are restricted by high borrowing costs, rising debt burdens, and limited access to affordable long-term financing. Tanzania stresses that improvements must be made to ensure expansion of concessional financing, mobilization of private investment, improved access to development and climate finance, and giving developing countries a stronger voice in the global financial decision-making. It is without a doubt that political commitment is paramount in undertaking focused investment. In that, Tanzania has made significant strides in reducing maternal and child mortality by expanding facility delivery from 51% in 2015 to 81% in 2022. Our experience on this demonstrates that when we invest in feasible projects and remain people-centered, development can move from promises to measurable results. It is in this spirit that Her Excellency President Samia Suluhu Hassan accepted the responsibility of championing maternal and child health for the African Union. Under her leadership, Tanzania reduced maternal deaths by 80% in just seven years. We now aim to advance the three zeros. Zero preventable maternal and child deaths, zero home deliveries, and zero unvaccinated children. Our experience shows that this is an agenda that Africa can successfully achieve, but it will require sustained political leadership adequate financing and stronger partnerships. We therefore urge the international community to join us in giving this agenda a big push. Excellencies, our efforts to address climate-related challenges continue to face unjustifiable obstacles, mainly from those contributing significantly to greenhouse gas emissions. Global efforts to address climate challenges are being frustrated by withdrawal of financial contributions, supporting climate adaptation measures and initiatives by international and regional institutions, as well as individual states. Let us prioritize delivery on the pledges for climate action by increasing long-term concessional financing and development of newer technologies. On this agenda, Tanzania chose to address the just energy transition component through different measures. Some of these measures include implementation of the national renewable strategy that comprises of a 2, 115 megawatt Julius Nyerere hydro power project of 650 megawatts of solar and wind power projects. 130 megawatts of geothermal power projects and the National Clean Cooking Strategy which aims to ensure that 80% of households adopt clean working by the year 2034. In our efforts to reduce the use of fossil fuels, we have also opted for the electric railway to link the port of Dar es Salaam to neighbouring countries of Burundi and the Democratic Republic of Congo. We therefore appeal that climate financing be provided as grants and concessional financing to step up efforts on climate action. Mr. President, Tanzania joins small island and coastal states in pushing for a workable solution to address sea level rises. We commend the President for convening today the high-level event addressing the existential threats posed by sea level rise, and we look forward to the adoption of the UN Declaration on Sea Level Rise, which will provide a comprehensive framework for international cooperation, scientific advancement, adaptation resilience, and legal stability. We welcome the declaration's legal affirmation on the stability of maritime zones under United Nations Convention on Law of the Seas and the continuity of statehood, even in cases of physical land loss, while encouraging strengthened international cooperation and the protection of human rights. Timely and urgent action is needed to safeguard the future of our coastal communities and island nations. Excellencies, global solidarity must be concurrent with respect of each other's sovereignty. Tanzania stands against the proliferating trend of some states to assume the responsibility of policing and imposing unilateral sanctions on others, thus undermining the principles of sovereignty and peaceful coexistence. As stated previously, Tanzania reaffirms its position to oppose the use of such coercive measures against any Member State and reaffirms its unwavering solidarity with Cuba, Zimbabwe and all other States that are subjected to such unjustifiable constraints. In line with this, our resolve to leave no one behind, we call for an immediate and unequivocal lifting of these measures that cause hardship, constrain development, and obstruct full enjoyment of human rights. Mr. President, global peace and security are vital for sustainable socioeconomic development. The United Nations, through its Charter, has remained central to international efforts to maintain peace and security, uphold international law, promote conditions conducive to development. However, despite these long-lasting commitments, the persistence of armed conflicts around the world reflect the departure from the purpose and principles of the Charter. In addition, there are emerging challenges to the authority of the United Nations Charter and the established principles of international law, often without commensurate accountability. These developments underscore the urgent need to reaffirm multilateralism, strengthen respect for international law, and reinforce the central role of the United Nations in maintaining international peace and security. In that regard, Tanzania remains firmly committed to supporting the efforts of the UN Security Council to fulfill its primary responsibility for the maintenance of international peace and security. Our commitment is demonstrated by our two terms of service on the Security Council during which we made substantive contributions to such cause. Notable achievements include the adoption of Security Council resolution 1653 in the year 2006 on the Great Lakes region and Tanzania's collaboration with Denmark in establishing the Peacebuilding Commission. Excellencies, Building on this record and sustained commitment to multilateralism, I am pleased to inform you that recently, the African Union formally took note of Tanzania's candidacy for a non-permanent seat on the UN Security Council for the term 2029-2030 during elections to be held by this Assembly in June 2028. I therefore seize this opportunity to formally announce our candidature. During our tenure in the Council, we will put forward and prioritize deliberations on matters vital to the maintenance of international peace and security such as preventive diplomacy and the peaceful settlement of disputes, women in peacekeeping, youth in peace and security, and the reform of the United Nations peacekeeping. In the coming days, we will engage with each one of you and present our vision and respectfully seek your valued support to enable Tanzania to serve with a strong African voice, principled leadership, and unwavering commitment to international peace and security. Mr. President, Tanzania is deeply concerned and saddened by the protracted conflict and humanitarian suffering in Gaza and across the Middle East. We continue to call for the protection of civilians, unhindered humanitarian assistance, and renewed diplomacy towards lasting peace. Tanzania remains firmly committed to the two-state solution, with Israel and Palestine living side by side in peace and harmony, in accordance with international law and relevant UN resolutions. We reaffirm the right of the Palestinian people to self-determination, and believe that lasting peace must guarantee dignity, security, and legitimate aspiration of both peoples. We have been consistent on this for the past 50 years. For us, this is a matter of our foreign principle. Mr. President, on behalf of the people of the United Republic of Tanzania, I wish to pay tribute to His Excellency Antonio Guterres as he concludes his distinguished tenure as Secretary-General of the United Nations. During his tenure, he steered the UN through an exceptionally challenging period marked by conflicts, geopolitical tensions, the COVID-19 pandemic, climate emergencies, and growing pressure on multilateralism. In all these situations, he remained firm and undeterred. Tanzania appreciates his support for Africa's aspirations for peace, sustainable development, climate justice, and a fairer international financial architecture, as well as his personal engagement with our country. Similar accolades are for Ambassador Amina Mohammed, Deputy Secretary-General, who has played a pivotal role in advancing the SDGs, advocacy for women, children, and those whose voices are too often unheard. We shall miss your contribution, but Africa is proud to welcome its own daughter back home. To both of you, we wish you every success and fulfillment in the years ahead. Mr. President, in conclusion, I wish to underscore that the UN must not merely reflect on the balance of power, but serve as a platform for justice, solidarity, and progress. As we take stock of its invaluable contribution to the advancement of humanity, maintenance of international peace and security, socio-economic progress and sustained development over the past 81 years, let us be reminded that there are more mountains to climb and milestones to accomplish. Tanzania believes that it is only by respecting and living by the Charter that we can honour the past and build a safer and better future for all. Thank you for your attention. Asante Sana.

GAPGA

On behalf of the Assembly, I wish to thank the Vice President of the United Republic of Tanzania.

The Assembly will now hear an address by His Excellency, Sirling Tshering Tobgay, Prime Minister of the Kingdom of Bhutan. I request protocol to escort His Excellency and invite him to address the Assembly.

BhutanPrime Minister

Mr. President, Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen, I stand before you today not as a Prime Minister, but as a salesman. And I am here not to sell you a product, or a policy, or yet another declaration. I am here to sell you An idea. An idea conceived and spearheaded by His Majesty King Jigme Khesar Namgyel Wangchuck. An idea embraced by the people of Bhutan. An idea already being built. That idea is Gyalpo Mindfulness City. And my sales pitch is simple. Come and build it with us. Now, the world has built new cities before. Financial centers, free ports, technology hubs, special economic zones. But GMC is different. You see, Gailipoo Mindfulness City is a special administrative region, an SAR. Under its royal charter, GMC exercises full autonomy in governance, legislation, and the judiciary. Think one country, two systems. Think of the agility of a microstate. But GMC was not inherited from history. It was not created to manage a transfer of sovereignty. It is being deliberately created by Bhutan, within Bhutan, on sovereign Bhutanese territory for the future. GMC covers more than 4,000 square kilometers. That is more than five times the size of Singapore. But its greatest opportunity is not its size. Its greatest opportunity is an institutional blank slate. GMC was given something extraordinarily rare, the freedom to design an entire city and its operating systems from first principles. So we asked, If you could begin again, how would you govern? What laws would you write? How would we regulate business? How would we guarantee an independent judiciary? How would we attract the best talent? How would we use technology and especially artificial intelligence? How would we create wealth while protecting nature? And ultimately, what would all that prosperity before. These were not theoretical questions. We answered them. And we are making full use of that institutional blank slate. If Singapore has legal principles that work, we learn from Singapore. If Abu Dhabi has financial regulations that work, we learn from Abu Dhabi. If leading jurists from the United Kingdom can help us build an independent jury, judiciary, we learn from them. And if international experts can strengthen our institutions, we learn from them. The principle is simple. Search the world for what works. Take the best, adapt it, and make it work for GMC. The result is a core operating system that is now in place. designed to give investors clarity, familiarity, and predictability. But GMC's operating system was designed around a deeper conviction that prosperity and values should reinforce one another. That means rejecting the assumption that we must choose between enterprise and well-being, between technology and humanity, between development and nature. At GMC, we believe a balanced approach can deliver substantial profits while protecting the values that makes prosperity worthwhile. Balance is not the enemy of profit. It is the foundation of lasting profit. And at GMC, Balance is not a slogan. It is built into the operating system. And this matters deeply to Bhutan. You see, Bhutan is peaceful and stable. Our forests are intact. Our culture is alive. Our people are educated. But our economy is small. It cannot yet create enough opportunities for our young people. So too many of them leave home to find opportunity elsewhere. For a country as small as ours, this is not only an economic challenge, it is an existential one. We cannot simply tell them to stay. We must give them a reason to stay and a reason to return. Jobs, opportunities, enterprise, a future. So Bhutan must transform. But we refuse to believe that transformation requires us to become somebody else. We want economic growth. We want investment. We want technology. We want successful companies. We want our people to become wealthier. But we also want to protect what makes Bhutan, Bhutan. That is the driving force behind His Majesty's vision for GMC. And that is why His Majesty is personally spearheading its development. GMC is not a project on the margins of Bhutan. It is at the heart of our national transformation. Our people have embraced GMC as a people's project, an investment in our children, our economy, and our shared future. Bhutan is not waiting to see whether the world believes in GMC before committing to it. We have committed, fully. Now let me tell you why GMC is built to succeed. Begin with location. GMC sits directly on the border with India, our closest friend and neighbor. The vision enjoys the support of Prime Minister Narendra Modi, the government of India, and our neighbors across the border in Assam. Beyond that border lies the world's most populous country and one of its largest and fastest growing economies. GMC is also a gateway to the markets of South Asia and Southeast Asia. So GMC begins with what many new cities spent decades trying to acquire. Access to vast and growing markets, connectivity, and in India, a trusted friend. Bhutan brings another advantage, one that cannot be bought. Trust. Trust built through peace, political stability, the rule of law, and a record for honoring our commitments. For long-term investors, trust creates something invaluable. Predictability. Bhutan has spent generations building that trust. GMC puts it to work. Then there is nature. Imagine GMC in the morning. Mist rising from its rivers. forest stretching towards the mountains, elephants moving through the landscape, tigers still roaming its forest. This is not empty land. It is a living, carbon-negative landscape, a biodiversity hotspot. We will not build over it. We will build within it and protect it. The forests, rivers, and wildlife of GMC are not obstacles to development. They are part of its value. And then there's energy. Bhutan is expanding its renewable energy capacity towards 25 gigawatts by 2040. That electricity will power GMC and the industries of the future. advanced manufacturing, scientific research, artificial intelligence and data centers, clean renewable power. But GMC has another type of power, a power Bhutan has cultivated for centuries, spiritual power. GMC is being developed as a global center for Vajrayana Buddhism. Spiritual masters from across the Buddhist world are already building monasteries, retreat centers, libraries, and institutions of learning. So imagine what will exist side by side. Entrepreneurs and monks. Artificial intelligence and human consciousness. Data centers and meditation centers. The newest technology humanity has created alongside some of the world's oldest traditions for understanding the human mind. Is that a contradiction? No. In fact, that is the point. GMC is not asking investors to choose between commercial success and quality of life. It is designed for both. Because the world's best people choose more than a workplace. They choose where to build their lives. Taken together, these advantages create the conditions for businesses to grow and investors to prosper. Lower uncertainty, abundant clean energy, access to growth, the ability to attract global talent and the freedom to create the markets others will later enter. That is how GMC turns its values into commercial advantage. Now you may reasonably ask, it sounds wonderful, but is it real? Yes, it is real. The Royal Charter is in force. Laws have been enacted. Regulators are operating. The framework for an independent judiciary is in place. GMC has its own government, its own laws, its own financial systems, and its own gold-backed digital currency. These are not aspirations. They are foundations already in place. The physical city is also taking shape. Infrastructure is being built progressively as and when it is needed. The international airport is under construction. A railway connection to India's vast rail network is being developed. Energy, digital connectivity, and urban infrastructure are being added as demand grows. Artificial intelligence and data center projects are moving forward, and nearly $5 billion in projects are under active negotiation. GMC is not an idea waiting to begin. The journey has begun. But there is still an extraordinary opportunity to help define where it goes. And perhaps the best way to understand GMC is to imagine it as a startup. a 4,000 square kilometre start-up. Now, most start-ups begin with an idea, then search for the conditions they need to succeed. GMC begins with many of them already in place: His Majesty's leadership, an entire country fully committed, land and clean energy, full autonomy, trusted laws and institutions, access to vast and growing markets. So GMC is a startup designed from the beginning for success. And there is one guarantee I can give you. Bhutan will not hedge its bets. We are all in. But every startup needs one more critical ingredient, co-founders. And that, Excellency, is why this salesman is standing before you. We want your capital, your technology, your talent, your ideas, your enterprise. And let me be absolutely clear. We want you to make money. GMC is not a retreat from capitalism, technology, or ambition. It is designed to harness all three without sacrificing nature, culture, or human well-being. Those who come early can help create the industries and markets that others will later enter. They can help define GMC's economic journey and share in the value they create. That is a first mover advantage. At GMC, Commercial success and human flourishing are designed to build on one another. This balance is deeply Bhutanese. For more than half a century, Bhutan has pursued gross national happiness. It does not reject economic growth, but it does ask the essential question, what is growth for? GMC gives this development philosophy contemporary form through markets, technology, and investment. But that aspiration itself is older. For centuries, the Himalayan Buddhist world has carried an ideal of an enlightened society, where material prosperity and spiritual wisdom coexist, where good governance serves human flourishing, and where people live in harmony with one another and with nature. That ideal is called Shambhala. Some of our spiritual masters have looked at what is taking shape in GMC and have said, "Under an enlightened king, Shambhala is being built." Now we make no claim to perfection. For us, Shambhala points not back to the past, but forward, a promise to carry its wisdom to the future, to build a city that prospers and has a soul. Mr. President, I told you at the beginning that I come here as a salesman. Now you know what I am selling. Kefu Mindfulness City. So to governments and institutions seeking partnership, and to investors, entrepreneurs, and companies seeking the next great opportunity, do not watch GMC being built. Come to Bhutan. Come to GMC. Help define the journey. Build it with us. Become our co-founders. Because the future does not simply arrive. The future is built. And in Bhutan, we are already building it. Thank you for your kind attention and Tashi Delek.

GAPGA

On behalf of the Assembly, I wish to thank the Prime Minister of the Kingdom of Bhutan. The assembly will hear and address by her excellency Kamla Prasad Besisa. Prime Minister of the Republic of Trinidad and Tobago. I request protocol to escort her excellency and invite her to address the assembly.

Trinidad and TobagoPrime Minister

Thank you very much, Mister President. I'm honored to again address this august chamber at this 81st session of the UN General Assembly. On behalf of the government and people of Trinidad and Tobago, I extend warmest congratulations to you on your election to the presidency. Permit me to extend also our appreciation to your predecessor, Her Excellency, Mayor Baak of Germany, for astute leadership in guiding our work in the previous session. Mr. President, this year, the theme chosen is a very apt one, that being restoring trust, managing transformation, and United Nations that delivers for all speaks directly to the challenges confronting the community today. And looking forward to restoring trust in the UN, we must understand we depend largely on the organization's ability to respond effectively to the needs of the entire global community. At a time when we should be strengthening partnerships, through mutual respect and cooperation, confidence in international institutions is under strain. For small developing states such as ours, trust depends on institutions applying agreed rules consistently, honouring commitments, and ensuring that those most affected by decisions have a meaningful voice in shaping them. Transnational organized crime, continues to pose a serious threat to the security and development of small island states. Small states face serious challenges from sophisticated criminal networks that move people, that move weapons, that move narcotics, and illicit finance across national borders. For Trinidad and Tobago, this is not an abstract threat. These networks directly endanger our citizens, they endanger our institutions, and they endanger our development. Restoring trust and managing transformation, therefore, must ultimately be about results. Ideally, the transformation that is required involves a United Nations that is responsive, that is effective and capable of making tangible differences to the safety, security, and well-being of people. Since my government was elected to office in 2025, we have pursued a people-centered agenda focused on safer communities, productive investment, modern public services, and expanded opportunity. A central part of our agenda has been restoring security to our communities. To this end, we have strengthened cooperative efforts with the United States and other partners to dismantle criminal syndicates that have wreaked havoc across our country and across our region. This is why we have profound gratitude to President Trump for his invitation to Trinidad and Tobago earliest year to be part of the newly formed shield of the Americas and America's counter cartel coalition. Remain confident that this partnership will continue to promote freedom, security, and prosperity in our region. Trinidad Tobago appreciates and recognizes the responsibility bestowed on the Security Council. In this regard, we extend our deepest appreciation to the 181 Member States that entrusted Trinidad and Tobago with the responsibility of serving on the Security Council for 2027-2028. Can we say thank you to all 181 States? We regard that overwhelming expression of confidence not simply as an achievement, but we see it as a very solemn responsibility on the part of Trinidad and Tobago. We return to the council for only the second time in the history of our nation. And this is for the first time in more than four decades. We will carry to the council the commitment on which we sought your support. We did so and we committed to building consensus for realization of sustainable peace and security. The Republic of Trinidad and Tobago intends to bring the perspective and experience of a small island developing state to the council. Whilst remain guided by the UN Charter by international law and the principle of the peaceful settlement of disputes. We will bring those principles to every matter before the council. whether the crisis lies within our region or far beyond it. We will approach our tenure with an independent and practical outlook, working constructively with all members of the Council and seeking common ground wherever possible. We intend to place particular emphasis on the curbing of the illicit trafficking of small arms and light weapons. Another pillar on which we had campaigned and we intend to commit to is women and children, as well as peace and security. And then we had talked about artificial intelligence and global security. Today, I want to agree with President Trump that we are now talking about a call for practical AI to be renamed super intelligence, SI. We commit to that. Mr. President. The illicit flow of firearms and narcotics is a major security concern for Trinidad and Tobago and the wider Caribbean. Although the region doesn't manufacture these weapons, the availability fuels gun violence, organized crime, drug trafficking, and loss of life across our societies. While serving on the council, Trinidad and Tobago will advocate for greater international cooperation to address the sources, movement and diversion of illicit weapons, stronger tracing mechanisms, information sharing, border and maritime cooperation, and deeper cooperation among source, transit and destination countries to disrupt weapons, narcotics and illicit financial flows. Shrinanta Bager will bring the experience of the Caribbean to the Council, where the impact of illicit farms demonstrates how transnational organized crime can threaten the security and stability of states, even in the absence of traditional armed conflict. On the priority area of superintelligence and global security, Shrinanta Bager will encourage a greater consideration of the implications of SI and emerging technologies for international peace and security, including cyber attacks, disinformation and deepfakes, autonomous weapons, criminal misuse of AI, and threats to critical infrastructure. We acknowledge that these technologies can support conflict prevention, early warning, peacekeeping, and protection of civilians. Trinidad and Tobago will advocate for an approach that safeguards international security without closing off innovation, development, and opportunity, and that ensures developing countries have a meaningful role in shaping the rules for this new technological era. Mr. President, the situation in Haiti remains of particular concern, not just for us in the region, but, I think, across the world. Trinidad and Tobago stands in full support of international efforts to help restore security and stability in Haiti whilst maintaining that the country's political future must ultimately be Haitian-led and Haitian-owned. Security assistance is necessary, but lasting stability will also require functioning institutions, economic opportunities, and a credible political process. So therefore, Therefore, as Trinidad and Tobago prepares to serve on the Security Council, we will continue to bring attention to Haiti and to the wider security concerns of the Caribbean, whilst working with CARICOM and other international partners towards practical and sustainable solutions. Mr. President, managing transformation must also mean ensuring that developing developing countries are not simply expected to adjust the changes decided or developed elsewhere. Whether in technology and SI, super intelligence, a global economy, or energy development countries must have the opportunity and the capacity to help in shaping those changes. Trinidad and Tobago brings a distinctive perspective as we understand that Affordability and economic development must advance together. For us in Trinidad and Tobago, progress cannot be measured only by how quickly the world changes, but it must also be in terms of who benefits from that change. Consequently, the transformation should create greater opportunity, strengthen security, and support development. rather than deepen inequality, indebtedness or dependence. Restoring trust in the United Nations will depend on its ability to deliver on the commitments already made and to demonstrate that multilateralism can make a meaningful difference in the lives of people. Mr. President, the Secretary-General's UN80 initiative to make the organisation more efficient and better equipped for the future is necessary and timely. Indeed, today, as we listened to President Trump, the Honourable President shared with us some of the initiatives for reform that was taking place and will take place here at the UN. Reform should reduce duplication, strengthen accountability, retire mandates that no longer serve their purpose, and direct scarce resources towards measurable results. At the same time, reform should preserve the organization's ability to deliver across its three pillars of peace and security, development and human rights, and should not make it more difficult for small states to participate meaningfully in its work. Mr. President, as the UN begins its search for its next Secretary-General, I take this opportunity to convey our deepest appreciation to His Excellency Antonio Guterres, whose term as the ninth Secretary-General of the UN concludes at the end of this year. Secretary-General Guterres will be well remembered for leading this organization through a period of extraordinary global strain, and for advancing important initiatives on UN reform, climate change, superintelligence and the risks posed by nuclear weapons. We also recognise some of the important initiatives advanced during his tenure, including the UN 80 Initiative efforts to achieve greater gender parity in senior UN leadership positions, and his efforts to bring superintelligence and the risks posed by nuclear weapons more firmly into the international agenda. Mr. President, as I close, I say that Trinidad and Tobago's longstanding commitment to multilateralism and the United Nations has been anchored in delivering results and adding value to the lives of citizens everywhere. As we chart our way forward, it is important for us all to remember that trust must be earned and build on the principles of mutual respect and cooperation. The Republic of Trinidad and Tobago is prepared to play its role and part to rebuild a United Nations that delivers for all. Mr. President, I thank you and may God continue to bless each and every one of you. Thank you very much.

GAPGA

On behalf of the Assembly, I wish to thank the Prime Minister of the Republic of Trinidad and Tobago. The Assembly will hear an address by Her Excellency, Takaichi Sanae, Prime Minister of Japan. I request protocol to escort Her Excellency and invite her to address the Assembly.

JapanPrime Minister

Madam President, Excellencies, The international order is experiencing a period of great instability. The free and open international order based on the rule of law that we have fostered is facing difficult challenges on multiple fronts. Amid a shifting balance of power and intensifying geopolitical competition, innocent civilian lives are being lost around the world every day. The stable post-Cold War era is now a thing of the past. The distribution of goods is stagnating. People across the world are suffering from high cost of living. Progress towards development goals is not on track, and human rights issues are rising in various places around the world. Against this backdrop, has the United Nations, now 80 years on since its foundation, been failing to fulfill its role in promoting peace and stability around the world? We are even hearing such concerns today. Madam President, Despite these concerns, the United Nations has never been more important than it is today in bringing about peace and stability to the world and enabling the international community to overcome new challenges and prosper. Japan will continue to fulfill its significant responsibilities towards the United Nations, and I am here today to express that resolve. This year marks the 70th anniversary of Japan's accession to the United Nations. In this milestone year, I would first like to address how Japan has been tackling the challenges facing the international community, working hand in hand with the United Nations. Then, together with you all, I would like to take this opportunity to revisit the role of the United Nations in the international community. Madam President, first, Let us turn our attention to escalating international tensions. The situation in the Middle East has been growing increasingly tense, and free and safe navigation is increasingly under challenge in the Strait of Hormuz, which is an international public good. Japan, in cooperation with the international community, has been continuing to engage in diplomatic efforts with a view to achieving an early de-escalation of the situation across the Middle Furthermore, supply concerns regarding fuel, chemical products, and medical supplies are causing significant impact on people's lives and business operations. Due to disruptions in the supply of fertilizers, the risk of food crisis is mounting, with Africa and Asia being hit particularly hard. For many years, we have engaged in dynamic trade in the free and open seas spanning the Pacific Ocean to the Indian Ocean, and together we have built a strong and prosperous region. This holds true also in the Atlantic Ocean and Mediterranean Sea. We wish to extend this to Africa as well to turn it into a main artery for growth and prosperity. To that end, Exactly 10 years ago, former Prime Minister Abe Shinzo advocated a free and open Indo-Pacific, FOIP, at the Tokyo International Conference on African Development, TICAD, held in Kenya. However, due to the recent intensification of geopolitical tensions, free trade has been hampered, and stable energy supplies and supply chains in general have been disrupted. Amid this situation in May this year, I announced the updated Free and Open Indo-Pacific, FOIP. There, I appealed that it is essential for countries to acquire the capabilities to freely determine their own futures and resilience across economic, social, and security domains. Japan places particular emphasis on following three pillars that embody this idea. First, Japan is engaged in strengthening the resilience of supply chains for energy and critical minerals. For global energy security, It is crucial to ensure free and transparent energy trade, engage in international coordination on strengthening oil stockpiling, and enhance collaboration between producing and consuming countries. Japan has also launched the Partnership on Wide Energy Resources Resilience Asia, Power Asia, to strengthen energy and resource supply resilience in Asia and has been promoting cooperation in areas such as stockpiling capacity development, and credit provision. Furthermore, Japan is currently formulating a comprehensive cooperation plan aimed at strengthening the economic and energy resilience of Gulf countries in the Middle East. Through this initiative, we will work to further strengthen the collaboration between the Asia-Pacific region, including Japan, and the Gulf countries to ensure a stable global energy supply. Moreover, concerns about arbitrary export restrictions are growing throughout the international community. Japan is proposing a vision for strengthening supply chains, which encompasses not only the development of alternative supply chains, supply sources, but also the enhancement of countries' ability to respond to supply disruptions, in particular in the field of critical minerals. One example is the resilient and inclusive supply chain enhancement partnership, RISE. Under this initiative, we are cooperating with countries that produce critical minerals to enable them to play a greater role in mining, refining, and processing. In June, we established RISE Plus under the World Bank Group and pledged a contribution of 20 million US dollars to help develop the infrastructure essential for critical minerals production. Second, Japan is devoted to enhancing cooperation towards peace and stability. Since the end of the Second World War, Japan has consistently and seriously pursued efforts towards nuclear disarmament and non-proliferation. At the very heart of our aspiration for a world without nuclear weapons lies the earnest plea of the hibakusha. catastrophic consequences of nuclear weapons must never be repeated. It is Japan's mission, as the only country to have ever suffered atomic bombings during war, to lead the efforts of the international community towards a world without nuclear weapons. Japan strongly calls for solidarity within the international community to maintain and strengthen the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty regime, to which both nuclear weapons states and non-nuclear weapons states are parties. Further, Japan will persistently advance realistic and practical efforts, including enhancing the transparency of nuclear forces and promoting a deeper understanding of the realities of atomic bombings. The situations in Ukraine and North Korea have reminded the world of growing risks and threats posed by nuclear weapons. There are also concerns regarding the proliferation of nuclear and missile-related technologies through the strengthening of military cooperation between Russia and North Korea. The security of the Indo-Pacific and Euro-Atlantic is inseparable. The advancement of North Korea's nuclear and missile programs, as well as its use of malicious cyber activities, including cryptocurrency thefts, as a source of funding, are clear violations of relevant Security Council resolutions and pose a serious threat to international peace and security. The full implementation of Security Council resolutions under the principle of the complete denuclearization of North Korea is essential. Moreover, the issue of abductions by North Korea is an ongoing matter with lives at stake. The abductees are still denied their freedoms, and their families continue to suffer. This is a matter of grave concern not only for Japan but for the international community. As the abductees and their families are aging, the abductions issue must be resolved immediately. For the sake of the future of both Japan and North Korea, I am prepared to engage in dialogue and take concrete action to establish a mutually fruitful relationship in accordance with the Japan-DPRK Pyeongyang Declaration. Third, Japan will continue to contribute to the maintenance and development of a free and open international order based on the rule of law. Any attempts to unilaterally change the status quo by force or coercion are contrary to the principles enshrined in the Charter of the United Nations and must never be tolerated anywhere in the world. Russia's aggression against Ukraine is the most obvious example. A permanent member of the Security Council, which is with a special responsibility for international peace and security, has initiated an act of aggression against another country and has vetoed Security Council resolutions concerning its own actions. In this current situation, it must be said that the Security Council is not functioning for international peace. Since the end of Second World War, Japan, as a peace-loving nation, has attached great importance to the rule of law in the settlement of any disputes. This is demonstrated by Japan's consistent support for and its contributions of judges to various international judicial organizations, such as the International Court of Justice, the International Criminal Court, and the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea. With this in mind, we established a unit for peace mediation within the government of Japan in March of this year. Japan will play a more proactive role in the peaceful settlement of disputes. Furthermore, the maritime order based on the rule of law is currently being greatly shaken in the Strait of Hormuz. Ensuring free and safe navigation through the Strait of Hormuz for all vessels without additional costs, as has been the case, is extremely important not only for the security of the Middle East, but also for the stability of the global economy as a whole. Similarly, it is essential to ensure stability in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. Japan will continue to work closely with relevant countries and the International Maritime Organization, IMO, towards the maintenance of the maritime order in the Middle East.

Madam President, next I would like to set out Japan's efforts and commitments towards the United Nations and multilateralism. Since becoming a member state of the United Nations in 1956, Japan has acted decisively to address global challenges such as eradication of poverty, economic and social development, women's empowerment, climate change, and global health. We have done so through our official development assistance and have deepened our solidarity with the global south. To date, Japan has provided ODA totaling over 670 billion US dollars to developing countries and regions, and has dispatched almost 60,000 Japan Overseas Cooperation Volunteers to 99 countries. Additionally, Japan has been promoting initiatives towards achieving universal health coverage, UHC, across the globe. Since 1993, Japan has co-organized the TCAD together with United Nations. TCAD has served as a platform for reflecting Africa's voice in the Sustainable Development Goals, SDGs, and for Japan to first put forward the concept of VOIP. Africa is endowed with a dynamic young population and possesses enormous economic potential. Japan will continue to promote its diplomacy towards Africa so that Japan and Africa can become more resilient and prosperous together. For example, we will promote industrial development, job creation, and enhanced connectivity in Africa. Furthermore, next year, I will host the Pacific Islands Leaders Meeting, PIM, in Yokohama, Japan, which Japan has convened together with the Pacific Islands region since 1997. Japan aims to further deepen our collaboration with the Pacific Island countries region and promote the stability and prosperity of the region, including addressing common challenges such as maritime security and climate change. Several large scale disasters have occurred and continuously caused extreme damage around the world this year, including in Japan. Natural disasters are becoming more severe and frequent, Japan is striving to become the world's leading nation in disaster risk reduction. To share Japan's expertise and technology in disaster risk reduction and contribute to global efforts in this field, I appointed a new Minister of State for International Disaster Risk Reduction Cooperation in my cabinet reshuffle last week. I myself, in 2015, as Minister for Internal Affairs and Communications, attended the United Nations World Conference on Disaster Reduction, where the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction was adopted. Promoting this framework remains one of our top priorities to this day. It is in Sendai that Japan will host the Asia-Pacific Ministerial Conference on Disaster Risk Reduction in October next year. To protect the lives of present and future generations, all states must take serious action to tackle global warming. I believe that climate action and economic growth can go hand in hand. Japan has been advancing green transformation GX efforts with the goal of achieving net zero by 2050. Such capabilities include establishing the basis for the production and engineering of materials such as green steel, utilizing the world's most efficient gas fire power generation, and popularizing the adoption of energy efficient data centers. harnessing Japan's technological capabilities. We will enhance these efforts with a view to strengthening the resilience of the energy supply demand structure and vigorously advance the policy package for wide energy and resources resilience through green transformation or power GX. Furthermore, Japan will contribute to global climate action, including through GX related efforts such as the Asia Zero Emission Community. that simultaneously achieve decarbonization, energy security, and economic growth. Next year, Japan will host the World Horticultural Exposition 2027 in Yokohama, which is an industrial trade fair showcasing green technologies and approaches to sustainable development. We sincerely hope that many of you will come to join this expo. There are also challenges arising from technological innovation. While advances in AI bring tremendous opportunities for humanity, they also pose challenges, including those related to national security. We also urgently need measures to tackle the spread of information not based on facts, as well as the spread of propaganda. Japan took the initiative to launch the Hiroshima AI Process, establishing the world's first international world's first international principles and code of conduct to govern generative AI. In parallel, Japan has been working with like-minded partners and Global South partners to co-create a safe, secure, and trustworthy AI ecosystem and will enhance cooperation on safety to respond to the risks of highly capable frontier AI. To accelerate these efforts, we intend to host an AI summit in Japan at the earliest opportunity. Madam President, since the end of the Second World War, Japan has built the peace and prosperity it has today through the tireless efforts of our predecessors and the goodwill of a large number of countries. In the course of these efforts, Japan itself has consistently acted in the spirit of multilateralism towards addressing challenges facing the international community. However, these challenges cannot be solved by any single country acting alone. Now more than ever, the flag of the United Nations must be held high, and under that banner, member states must mobilize the collective strength of the membership to elaborate new rules and build a framework for cooperation. I am convinced that the United Nations is the only organization capable of taking the helm on a global scale. To this end as well, reform of the United Nations is essential. The United Nations is a vessel and the responsibility for determining its contents lies with us, namely the member states. Rather than lamenting the institutional fatigue of the United Nations, member states should unite with one heart, vigorously advance reform of the United Nations, and transform the organization into a more resilient and effective United Nations. Let us move forward, building on the achievements of the current Secretary-General, Antonio Guterres. At the same time, the Charter of the United Nations, which is now 81 years old, should also be reviewed. Regarding the so-called enemy states clauses, a United Nations General Assembly resolution was adopted in 2005 to delete references to enemy states from the Charter of the United Nations, expressing the resolve of the heads of state and government of all member states. In accordance with this resolution, these clauses must be deleted. I would like to strongly emphasize this position as Japan takes pride and honor in its significant contributions to the efforts of the United Nations for the last 70 years. Furthermore, as a matter of utmost importance, reform of the Security Council is urgently needed. The current structure of the Security Council, whose mandate is to maintain international peace and security, reflects the international situation as it stood in 1945. We need to transform it without delay into a structure that truly reflects the current realities of the international community. To this end, it is essential to expand the number of both permanent and non-permanent members in order to ensure the legitimacy and representativeness of the Security Council. A majority of member states support the expansion of both categories. Japan is determined to fulfill its solemn responsibility in these UN reforms. Madam President, in the 70 years since we became a UN member state, Japan has consistently contributed to the peace and prosperity of the international community as a peace-loving nation under its exclusively defense-oriented policy. Furthermore, we have worked hand in hand with United Nations on the two indispensable tasks of establishing rules and institutions and providing support on the ground. This policy will remain unchanged in the future. In light of this history, Japan feels a sense of responsibility to safeguard the ideals of the United Nations as our beacon of hope and to carry that light forward into the future. To that end, with its renewed commitment to the United Nations and multilateralism, Japan will continue to steadily take actions. Now, at a time when the world is in turmoil, the United Nations itself must be reborn as a more resilient and effective United Nations and regain the trust of the international community. Together with this more resilient and effective United Nations, Japan is determined to create peace and prosperity by making the Indo-Pacific and the international community more resilient and prosperous. Thank you so very much.

GAPGA

On behalf of the Assembly, I wish to thank the Prime Minister of Japan. The Assembly will hear an address by His Excellency Andy Burnham, Prime Minister and First Lord of the Treasury of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland. I request protocol to escort His Excellency and invite him to address the Assembly.

United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern IrelandPrime Minister

Madam President, Your Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen. As the new British Prime Minister, I'm here today to tell you how Britain will deliver leadership in a changing world for the decade that lies ahead, learning from our experience of the last one. It is now 10 years since Brexit. My country has lived through the disruption it brought, and it has given us a unique perspective that I want to share with you today. Britain is back. We are restoring our stability, building a more dynamic economy, a nation that wants to trade with the world and work together to solve the shared problems we face. But we have also learned that we need to adapt to meet the challenge of these times. We need to rebalance power in our country and bring it closer to people. We need to work harder to fight the forces of division and instability which threaten us. Not just through hard power, but through softer, slower means that sow fear and despair. We need to do more to help people with the everyday cost of living and seize the opportunities that give them hope for the future. And we need to embrace the incredible potential of technology to improve people's lives. That's what I want to talk to you about this evening, how the world can come through the turbulence of today to reach towards something better in the decade ahead. Overcoming the forces of division and instability starts with national security. So we will keep investing in our defence, meeting our NATO commitments and strengthening European capabilities. We will be relentless in building up our hard power and deterrence. But we will not play Russia's game of trading escalatory rhetoric. Unlike Russia, we do not seek confrontation. Instead, we will be prepared but not panicked, clear-eyed but cool-headed.

and unflinching in defending our people and our allies. True resilience depends on this military strength, but the last 10 years tells us that it is also about something deeper as well. It is about the strength of the social fabric that binds us together. There is no national security without a strong, cohesive society underneath it. That's the starting point for everything we hold dear and everything we want to achieve. But the fact is, it has been under attack. In recent years, we have seen industrial-scale assault by hostile actors on the information environment in the UK and that of many of our allies. Russian agencies have used every means at their disposal to spread lies and disinformation and prey on people's fears. They've used bots and fake websites, falsified newspaper articles, forged the branding of 28 British organisations, including universities and the BBC. They've amplified far-right narratives, And we have evidence that they tried to interfere with the 2019 general election. We also know that they have tried to stoke tensions and unrest in the wake of horrific events. The idea that anyone would try to use such things to their advantage is just repulsive, but it is what they do. The Kremlin spends around 1.3 billion pounds each year on manipulating information. We're talking about an insidious campaign that reaches into people's homes and twists what they feel about their own country and community, creating a narrative of decline, stoking division, and sowing despair. On top of that, we have seen cyber attacks on companies and institutions, and we know that AI will multiply the threat. We have tiptoed around this for too long. Over the last decade, we have given too much ground to those who want to run a negative, corrosive narrative about life in Britain, which bears no resemblance to reality. Well, no more. We are going to face the new decade in a different way, with our eyes wide open. We are going to be much prouder in standing up for our values and the rule of law, and we are going to help our people to strengthen their resilience Because faced with this information warfare, security starts in every home. If you're struggling with the cost of living and your life is not improving, or if you're a young person not in employment, education or training, you are going to be much more vulnerable to this kind of influence. So part of the challenge is to lift our people up and create the opportunities they need. When inequalities grow too wide, our societies are at greater risk. So we will work to make life more affordable for people. That will be at the heart of a new 10-year plan for Britain that we will bring forward later in the year. And we will put in place the architecture to stem this poisonous tide. Today, I am asking our security chiefs in the UK to begin work on a new National Centre for Information Defence. to detect, attribute, and disrupt these kinds of hostile state information attacks, to support and defend our democracy. I know this is a shared challenge, so we are going to use our experience in the UK and the fact that we have already been through this shock, starting 10 years ago, to help other countries. We have already supported Moldova to protect its elections from Russian interference. As more elections approach across Europe, more nations are grappling with these issues, some for the first time. So we're ready to share our understanding of how these actors work and how we can respond, because this is a vital task for our collective security and resilience. To overcome division and instability, we must also find new ways to bring countries together. We know that we are at our strongest when we unite with others, when we reach across borders to solve shared problems. Standing here today, I am reminded of the huge human progress that this organization has led, like the eradication of smallpox or the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. That is the kind of promise and hope that led Britain to host the very first meeting of this General Assembly in London, and led to the world to create this institution, these United Nations, our United Nations. That is the level of ambition that we need now to renew the UN for our times, to tackle challenges like improving global health and preventing future pandemics, to end the wars that are causing so much suffering and instability, including the terrible conflict in Sudan, and to tackle climate change. The climate crisis is now a national security threat for countries around the world, as this summer of extreme heat, wildfires, and floods has proved beyond doubt. Britain will continue to lead with others to fight this threat, to protect our children and grandchildren, to protect the natural world, and also to seize the benefits for jobs, growth, and reindustrialization that the clean energy transition can bring. So we must raise our sights. And I believe the United Kingdom has a unique position as an honest broker to help drive this forward. We are America's closest ally. We have deep ties with our friends in the European Union and seek to deepen them further. We work with China and emerging powers like India and Brazil. We sit on the UN Security Council, in the Commonwealth, in the CPTPP. In a divided world, we have the ability to bring people together And we will. We are going to step into that role and we are going to start with one of the most significant challenges and opportunities of our age, frontier AI. AI brings together so many of the most pressing issues before us. It is already speeding up cancer diagnosis in the UK, but AI has the potential to go further, not just to help prevent and treat cancer, but to help cure it. AI will also be the key to economic growth, the route to transforming education, and it will be a vital tool to keep us safe. I am announcing today that we are developing a new AI defense partnership with the United States to protect our critical national infrastructure. But we know that AI will also be a source of disruption to the way we live and work, a multiplier of risk. We've all heard the warnings, which we must heed. I know how worried people are, so we have to rise to this moment. Fundamental decisions on this technology are too important to be left to chance. They must be taken by elected governments who serve working people. and we need to give people the support they need through this change, ensuring that it becomes an engine for reindustrialisation and opportunity as well. There is a lesson from the first industrial revolution, which started in northern England two centuries ago. It was a time of incredible technological progress, but for workers, the disruption brought huge suffering and exploitation. Things got a lot worse before they got better. So this time, we need to get it right. I believe we're more than equal to the task. The UK has some of the best tech and AI talent anywhere in the world. And when it comes to guarding against the risks, we have our world-leading AI Security Institute, working hand in glove with the US and the leading labs on AI safety. But we need to go further. Building on the meeting convened by His Majesty King Charles last week, I can announce today that I am going to put AI at the heart of the UK's G20 presidency next year. I look back at how we responded to the financial crisis back in 2008. We moved quickly in the G20 and smaller groups to deliver an urgent, practical response. We came together to agree principles which everyone implemented at home in a way that was right for them, and it worked. That is the kind of approach we need now. So we will bring the right people together on the key issues, delivering on the potential of AI for good and dealing with the risks. And we will work towards agreeing a single set of global principles and standards to ensure the transparency and access we need to increase our preparedness and to ensure that AI development is safe. This will bring together welcome initiatives from others, like that proposed by Norway this week. As His Majesty said, the task before us is not merely to advance technology, but to ensure that it remains firmly in the service of humanity. And I want to reassure the British people that ultimately, we will do whatever is necessary to protect them, including bringing forward new laws if that is what is needed. They need to know that we will protect their interests, and we will. But on its own, that's not enough, is it? In this dangerous, turbulent age, it is more important than ever that we give people the power to build their own resilience and do more for themselves. and give them the platform to stand up for what they believe in. I am working to rebalance power across all regions of the UK. And as part of that, I have set up a second Downing Street office in Manchester. We call it Number 10 North. Outside that office stands a statue of Abraham Lincoln. It marks the personal connection he made with Manchester and the bond between our two nations. a bond which he described in a letter to the working people of the city as perpetual. This was not due to some military or material support. There was no quid pro quo. It was because Manchester's humble mill workers took a principled stand. During the American Civil War in 1862, despite the hardships it brought them, they refused to touch raw cotton that had been picked by slaves. in 1862. People with little power used it to help those with none on the other side of the world. The best change is change like that, bottom-up change led by people. And whatever distorted view social media offers today, the world is still full of good and decent people all over the world who are ready to stand up for what is right. I see that shining through all the time. Nothing brings the British people together across age, race and class more than their hatred of injustice, the misuse of power against the powerless. We will always stand for the underdog against the bully. That's why we are so united behind Ukraine. And let me say, we salute the Ukrainian people. They are showing depths of resilience and courage. That is an inspiration to the whole world. I was in Kyiv last month, and it gave me a glimpse of life under Russian attack. I went to a bustling market, just a normal scene from any European city. The traders singing the praises of their products, pushing into my hands peaches and plums from Odessa. But their stalls were out on the street because the market hall had been destroyed. In the background, there were burned out cars. Behind us, a building that had taken a direct hit just a few weeks before. I met people riding the metro home from work, people just getting on with their lives. But at night, those same metro stations doubling as shelters for thousands of people, from the elderly to little kids, some who have known nothing but war. People told me about the freezing conditions in the stations last winter, when temperatures dropped below minus 20 degrees outside. Meanwhile, Russia was targeting their energy infrastructure, trying to make them suffer even more. We can't let them do that again this winter. So we're working to help Ukraine protect their skies and civilians. We're leading the charge in raising the cost for Russia of continuing this senseless and illegal war. The Graham bill, which President Trump signed last week, will make a huge difference to that effort. And we will support Ukraine to repair and protect the heat and power plants that Kyiv will depend upon this winter. It is right that we provide that support. But we should call Russia out this time and every time. Everyone in this room knows that strikes on civilian infrastructure are explicitly forbidden by international law. Yet we stand here in the UN announcing funding to mitigate the effects of these war crimes, which we reliably expect to be perpetrated yet again by a permanent member of the Security Council. It must end. Russia could choose a different course tomorrow, accept a ceasefire, come to the negotiating table. I urge them to do so. But until then, we will stand with Ukraine, stronger than ever, for as long as it takes. This is about upholding the UN Charter and the rule of law. We will stand firm in the face of any threats and challenges to the rule of law, not just from Russia, but from others too, including where they threaten the rights of British territories, to remain British, such as the Falkland Islands. That's why we're also working with France and other partners to support freedom of navigation in the Gulf. And it's why I have acted on the Middle East. Just eight weeks into becoming Prime Minister, working with my Foreign Secretary, Ed Miliband, I comprehensively reset our position. And we built an international coalition of countries to come with us. The terrorist attack on Israel on 7 October 2023 was utterly horrific. I have condemned it in the strongest possible terms. We continue to condemn Hamas, and we stand with Israel in the face of the ongoing threats, including from Iran, against Israel and Jewish people around the world. But this does not justify the Israeli Government's actions in Gaza or the West Bank. Far too many people have died, including so many children. Far too little aid is getting in. And it has gone on for far too long. We will not stand by as the horrific suffering continues to grow and the prospect of a two-state solution, the best hope for peace and stability for both nations, comes under attack. Last month, Israel issued tenders for the construction of the E1 mega settlement, which would drive a wedge through the West Bank and threaten to put a viable Palestinian state beyond reach. It cannot be allowed to happen. So we have acted by banning trade in goods with illegal settlements, recognising that the Israeli occupation of the Palestinian territory is unlawful, and sanctioning those taking part in the construction of illegal settlements. We want to see the suffering and death finally come to an end. We want to see Israeli and Palestinian people living side by side in peace and security. And we will do all we can to keep the hope of that possibility alive. And look, we live in an age of low trust in politics. If we were to continue to talk about the two-state solution, but fail to back those words with deeds, that trust will fall even lower and our enemies will seek to exploit the alienation that follows from that. We won't let it happen. So, your excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, this is the kind of leadership Britain is here to bring. We need to recommit together to make the decade ahead of us better than the last. My message to our partners around the world is this: you can count on us. Count on us to stand up for those long-standing British values of fairness and justice, our shared values, and for the UN Charter. Count on us to fight racism, discrimination and the abuse of power wherever we see it, just as those Manchester cotton workers did in the 19th century, and the country did in the fight against fascism in the 20th century. Count on us to bring people together, not to point towards old problems, but to work towards new solutions for the 21st century. Count on us to meet fear and division with unity and hope. Thank you very much indeed.

GAPGA

On behalf of the Assembly, I wish to thank the Prime Minister and First Lord of the Treasury of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland. The Assembly will hear an address by His Excellency, Andriy Plenkovic, Prime Minister of the Republic of Croatia. I request protocol to escort his Excellency and invite him to address the Assembly.

CroatiaPrime Minister

Good evening, Madam Chair, Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen. We come to this Assembly from countries that differ in size, population and power. Yet here, precisely because of that, every country has its unique experience to share, responsibilities to assume, and a contribution to make. Croatia brings the experience of a nation that within one generation endured aggression and occupation, defended its freedom, and rebuilt itself. It joined the UN, NATO, and the EU, and developed a flourishing democracy and a growing economy. Our path and our transition were neither straight or easy, but we made it. Over the past decade as Prime Minister, I have seen Croatia translate those experiences into progress at home and more responsibility abroad. They have reinforced three convictions that speak directly to the theme of this session. First, rules are our common compass. Second, Transformation help us build resilience. Third, trust is earned only through delivery. Ladies and gentlemen, we support rule-based multilateralism as the pinnacle of human cooperation, not because we are naive, but because we have seen and experienced the alternative. For smaller and medium-sized states, international law is not an abstraction. It is the line between order and tyranny, between sovereign equality and the rule of force. The rule of force, such as witnessed by Croatia during the brutal aggression and occupation of more than one quarter of our territory in the 90s, in the war which claimed nearly 20,000 lives, and after which, more than three decades later, Croatia continues to search for 1,725 missing persons, a poignant example that the consequences of war do not end when the weapons fall silent. Instead, peace requires courage, credible institutions, and rules that apply equally to everyone. Russia's ongoing war of aggression against Ukraine is a direct assault on those rules. Croatia will continue to support Ukraine's sovereignty, independence, and territorial integrity, and a comprehensive, just, and lasting peace based on the UN Charter. Peace cannot reward conquest, and recovery cannot be separated from justice. The same compass must guide us in the Middle East. Protection of civilians, unhindered humanitarian access, respect for international law, and a credible political horizon are essential to breaking the cycle of violence. Croatia supports a negotiated two-state solution in which Israelis and Palestinians will live in peace and security. From Sudan and Myanmar to the Sahel and the Great Lakes region, civilians bear the highest cost when rules are ignored and diplomacy fails. And no crisis remains local for long. War disrupts food and energy supplies, while insecurity from the Strait of Hormuz to the Black Sea affects shipping, prices and livelihoods across continents. This is why, as a government, we are dealing with the consequences of energy price pressures by passing degrees to protect Croatian citizens and economy from energy shocks created far away from our shores. As distant as they may seem, these shocks are real, as they ripple into domestic inflationary pressures, affecting everything from wages and pensions to food prices and basic services. This is why freedom of navigation, maritime security, and the strict implementation of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea matter to everyone. For us, freedom of navigation and maritime security are both a national interest and a global responsibility. Common rules do not hold us back. They provide the stability and predictability necessary for countries to advance their ambitions. The world is being transformed by technology, climate change, demographic pressures, illegal migration, and geopolitical rivalry. Our responsibility is to govern them so that change expands human freedom and security instead of weakening them. The United Nations must begin with its own transformation. Croatia supports a UN that is more effective, accountable and financially sustainable, and stronger across all three pillars: peace and security, sustainable development and, of course, human rights. Reform must also produce a more representative and effective Security Council. When the Council is blocked, the General Assembly can and must act, but it cannot replace the Council's primary responsibility under the Charter. This makes the selection of the next Secretary-General all the more relevant. I thank, therefore, Secretary-General Guterres for his work over the last decade. The United Nations needs leadership capable of bringing Member States together defending the Charter and turning reform into measurable results. No country alone can successfully respond to the global transformations we witness today. Artificial intelligence can accelerate development, but its use must remain consistent with legal frameworks, human dignity and democratic accountability. Renewed nuclear rhetoric makes a firm commitment to the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons more important than ever. Climate action should be used to strengthen energy security and social cohesion. Our experience shows that the green transition should not be ideological. It can endure only when it is technologically realistic, socially fair, compatible with secure and affordable energy, and supportive of overall development. For Europe, which imports most of the energy it consumes, the case for producing more renewable energy at home now reaches far beyond climate policy. It is a strategic necessity. It strengthens Europe's sovereignty and capacity to act, reduces external dependence, creates economic opportunity, and makes our societies more resilient. The same principle applies to illegal migration, which has caused mistrust in Europe and altered the political landscape in many countries. This situation is unacceptable and it cannot continue. The rule of law must be upheld and legal procedures must be followed. Our primary responsibility is to our citizens and it starts at our borders. We are not allowing uncontrolled migration and we are fighting the criminal networks that facilitate it. As an EU external border country, Croatia carries an additional responsibility and we will fulfill it with determination. Transformation is equally important in our own neighborhood. Southeast Europe remains the unfinished part of the European project. Croatia will continue to support merit-based EU enlargement. EU membership can turn borders of division into lines of cooperation, and reforms on paper into stronger institutions and better living standards. But European transformation requires honesty about the past. Reconciliation becomes possible when responsibility for the crimes of the past is acknowledged and their glorification rejected. That standard allows no national exceptions. That means respect for victims and clear rejection of historical revisionism, not the glorification of war criminals. Radko Mladic was a convicted war criminal responsible for the Srebrenica genocide, the first genocide in Europe since the Holocaust. While his criminal record reached its nefarious culmination in Srebrenica, his trail of war crimes stretches further back to the shelling of Croatian cities, the murder of civilians, the mining of dams, and the destruction of cultural heritage and industrial facilities. The military and official honours accorded to Mladic in Serbia were an affront to his victims and to the judgements of international courts. The participation of state representatives in the public claim that accompanied the ceremony is totally incompatible with the values of a union Serbia seeks to join. The same commitment to equality and reform should guide Bosnia and Herzegovina. As a signatory to the Dayton Peace Accords and a neighbor and a friend of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia is one of the strongest advocates of its European future. The Dayton Peace Accords ended the war and established the constitutional framework for Bosnia and Herzegovina, one state, two entities, and three constituent peoples: Croats, Bosniaks, and Serbs. That balance is the foundation on which peace was built. Yet the Croats of Bosnia and Herzegovina are still being denied legitimate representation, including in the presidency of the country. That is unjust. destabilizing and contrary to the spirit of Dayton. The solution is neither division nor domination. It is carefully designed electoral reform that protects every citizen while ensuring that a basic principle of legitimate political representation of the constituent peoples is restored. Croatia will not tire of explaining why this reform is crucial for the entire country to reach its full potential. and we will not tire of opposing those political forces whose short-sighted pursuit of political gains jeopardizes equality of constituent peoples and the long-term prosperity. Our own history confirms that transformation succeeds when it is rooted in inclusion, responsibility, and reform.
